fmcg-market-mexico:
This guide is a stand-alone reference for foreign manufacturers and suppliers that already sell successfully in their home or other export markets and want to introduce their brands or products into Mexico — whether under their own brand name or as a private label. It explains what the fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) sector covers, how large the Mexican market is, who the main players are, where the opportunities lie for newcomers, and what a foreign supplier must do to place goods on Mexican shelves.

The core of the guide is a directory of relevant Mexican FMCG importers and distributors — companies that have the connections to retail and HoReCa (hotels, restaurants, catering / foodservice) buyers and the capability to introduce new brands and products in volume. For each entry the directory gives the website, a general (non-personal) e-mail address, the switchboard / central telephone number where publicly available, and a direct link to the supplier or “become-a-supplier” page where one exists. It states whether the names of buyers or managers who decide on new-supplier listings appear on the company website, but — for data-protection reasons — it does not reproduce personal names or personal e-mail addresses.

Contact-quality note. Contact information changes frequently and its depth varies from company to company. Only companies with a working website and a verifiable public contact channel are listed. Where a firm publishes no central switchboard and channels new-supplier enquiries exclusively through an online form or supplier portal, the guide says so and gives that channel rather than an unverifiable number.
fmcg-market-canada:
This study is a stand-alone reference for international brand owners, manufacturers and exporters who are considering entering the Canadian market with fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG). It covers the full FMCG spectrum – both food and non-food – and focuses on the practical questions a supplier asks first: how large is the market, who are the leading players, where are the openings for new brand and private-label products, what does it take to get products across the border and onto Canadian shelves, and – most importantly – which Canadian importers and distributors are able and willing to introduce foreign products at scale.

FMCG importers and distributors deserve special attention because they hold the relationships that a newcomer lacks: they are already connected to retail chains, independents and – in many cases – the HoReCa/foodservice trade, and they can list and move new brands in large volumes, whether under the supplier's own brand or as private label. The directory in Section 8 profiles a set of relevant Canadian importers and distributors, each with a verified website and direct contact details.
horeca-foodservice-market-ireland:
Ireland's out-of-home market reached a record turnover of approximately €10.4 billion in 2025. For a foreign supplier the structure is unusually favourable: a handful of large broadline distributors reach the majority of operators, so securing a single national listing can open very wide coverage — a rare thing in European foodservice, where most markets require several regional partners before a product is genuinely available nationwide.

The Irish supply chain is dominated by those broadliners, supported by cash & carry networks, branded-goods distributors and category specialists. Sysco Ireland, incorporating the former Pallas Foods, is the largest foodservice distributor on the island, with a wide fresh, frozen, ambient and non-food range and next-day nationwide delivery. Musgrave MarketPlace is the leading wholesale supplier to foodservice, retail and SME customers, combining delivered wholesale with a national cash & carry branch network; BWG Foodservice, the wholesale division of BWG Foods (SPAR Ireland), serves tens of thousands of retail and hospitality customers; and La Rousse Foods is the leading premium and fine-food distributor to top kitchens. This study sets out market size and structure, the access requirements by supplier origin, and a directory of Irish importers and distribution partners.
horeca-foodservice-market-sweden:
The Swedish out-of-home profit sector — restaurants, hotels, cafés, bars, catering and travel — generated revenue of approximately SEK 163 billion (around USD 15 billion) in 2023. Two demand patterns matter for a new supplier. Kitchen labour is scarce and costly, which puts pre-prepared and portioned formats in structural demand; and retail alcohol is sold only through the state monopoly Systembolaget, so the on-trade is supplied separately by importers and distributors to licence-holding venues — a distinction that changes the route to market for any beverage supplier.

A foreign supplier can enter through four partner types, and choosing the right one determines who to contact and what they will expect. Broadline foodservice wholesalers carry thousands of food and non-food lines and deliver nationwide, which suits products that can achieve volume across many outlets. Cash & carry operators are a fast route to trial and to independent restaurants and cafés. Retail groups with wholesale and import arms buy for both retail and foodservice and run large private-label programmes. Brand importers and distributors specialise in bringing international brands and private label into Sweden. This study covers market size and structure, access requirements by supplier origin, and a directory of Swedish importers and foodservice distributors.
fmcg-market-czech-republic:
The Czech consumer goods market is compact but highly organised, and its retail is among the more concentrated in Central Europe: a handful of international chains and discounters account for most grocery volume, while cash & carry and delivered wholesale serve independent retail, HoReCa and resellers. For a foreign supplier the practical question is not volume but route — the market is easy to enter on paper and demanding in its listing and labelling requirements.

This study sets out the scope of the fast-moving consumer goods sector, measures and structures the market across food and non-food, profiles the leading retail and wholesale players, explains the access requirements for suppliers from the EU, from non-EU Europe and from outside Europe, and provides a directory of Czech FMCG importers and distributors.
fmcg-market-egypt:
Egypt is the most populous country in the Arab world and one of the largest consumer markets in the Middle East and Africa. For manufacturers and suppliers of fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) whose brands or products already sell successfully abroad, it offers a sizeable and growing outlet — provided the market is entered through the right local partner and in line with Egypt's import rules.

This study is written as a stand-alone reference for foreign suppliers. It explains what FMCG covers, sizes the Egyptian market, maps the main players and sales channels, sets out the market-access requirements (differentiated by the supplier's country of origin), highlights the product groups with the best sales prospects, and — as its central component — provides a classified directory of Egyptian FMCG importers and distributors that are able and willing to introduce foreign brands or private-label products into the market.

For each listed company the directory gives the website, a central (switchboard) telephone number, a general e-mail address where one is published, whether the company operates a dedicated channel for new suppliers, and a classification by channel type, by food vs. non-food, by product categories carried, and by whether the company sees itself primarily as a "brand-maker" (actively seeking new, innovative brands) or as a distributor of established, well-known brands and private label.

A note on personal data and data quality. For data-protection reasons this study does not list the names or personal e-mail addresses of individual buyers or managers. Where a company publishes a dedicated route for new suppliers (a purchasing/supplier e-mail, a "work with us" or import enquiry page), this is indicated so that suppliers can reach the right desk without personal contact details. Companies are only included where a website or direct contact data (telephone and/or e-mail) could be verified; the depth and freshness of published contact information varies from company to company, so details should always be reconfirmed before a first approach.
fmcg-market-japan:
This study is a stand-alone reference for international manufacturers of branded and private-label consumer goods that are considering, or preparing, entry into the Japanese market. It brings together the market context, the structure of Japanese retail and distribution, the practical requirements for placing food and non-food products on the shelf, and — at its core — a classified directory of importers and distributors with direct contact details.

The focus is fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG): everyday, frequently purchased, relatively low-priced products that sell in high volume and turn over quickly. In the food sphere this covers processed and packaged foods, confectionery and snacks, beverages, seasonings and alcoholic drinks. On the non-food side it covers cosmetics and personal care, over-the-counter "quasi-drugs" (functional health & beauty products — not prescription medicines), household and cleaning products, and pet supplies. Durable goods, electronics, apparel and fresh commodity produce are outside the scope.

Japan rewards preparation. It is one of the world's largest and most sophisticated consumer markets, but also one of its most demanding: quality is assumed rather than a differentiator, packaging and presentation matter greatly, and the route to retail runs through a layered distribution system in which the right partner is decisive. This study is designed to shorten that learning curve and to point suppliers directly to the companies that can carry their products.
baby-and-toddler-products-japan:
1. Executive Summary

Japan is a mature, shrinking-volume but high-value market for baby and toddler products. Births to Japanese nationals fell to a record low of 671,236 in 2025 (total fertility rate 1.14), yet spending per child remains among the highest in the world. Parents, and very often grandparents, buy fewer items but choose higher-quality, safer and better-designed products, which keeps value sales broadly stable while unit volumes decline. According to Yano Research Institute, the Japanese "baby-related business" market (products and services for children aged 0–2) reached JPY 4,657 billion in 2025 (+2.0%). Growth is driven by publicly subsidised daycare services, which account for the bulk of this figure, and by educational and infant toys; baby goods, baby food and baby apparel declined in 2025, partly cushioned by price increases. The wider toy market (all ages) set its sixth consecutive record at JPY 1,166.4 billion in fiscal 2025 (+6.3%), and the baby and children’s clothing retail market is worth about JPY 840 billion. For foreign suppliers the most important conclusions are: • Premium, design-led and safety-proven imports have a clear place. European brands (strollers, carriers, high chairs, wooden and educational toys, muslin and organic textiles) enjoy a strong image, particularly in department stores, select shops and online. • Private label is concentrated among a few large chains (Nishimatsuya, Akachan Honpo, Toys"R"Us/Babies"R"Us, AEON, Shimamura/Birthday, MUJI) that source largely from Asia; European suppliers compete here mainly with differentiated, certified products rather than on price. • Regulation has tightened substantially. Since 25 December 2025 toys for children under 3 and infant beds require the new Child PSC mark; strollers and bed guards followed on 8 July 2026. Mouth-contact toys and food-contact articles are regulated under the Food Sanitation Act. Japanese-language labelling and a Japanese importer of record are indispensable. • Market entry almost always runs through a specialised Japanese importer, typically as exclusive distributor (so-dairiten), because retailers buy only from suppliers with an existing account (kouza) and payment terms are long. • EU suppliers benefit from the EU–Japan EPA (duty-free on most relevant goods, e.g. baby apparel otherwise dutiable at roughly 6–11%). UK and Swiss suppliers have comparable agreements; suppliers from Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein or Turkey pay the normal WTO rates. Among non-European origins, ASEAN and CPTPP partners are largely duty-free, while China and Korea still face reduced but non-zero RCEP rates on apparel. Chapter 8 contains a directory of Japanese importers, distributors, wholesalers and directly importing retailers, structured by type and product focus, with website, supplier registration form where available, general e-mail address and switchboard number.
horeca-foodservice-market-united-kingdom:
The United Kingdom is one of the largest and most dynamic foodservice markets in Europe. Depending on scope and methodology, the total out-of-home market is valued at roughly US$100–111 billion (about £80–90 billion) across 2025–2026, and is forecast to keep growing at a mid-single-digit annual rate for the rest of the decade. For an exporter the attraction is not only the size of the market but its openness: a high share of imported food and drink, a settled appetite for world cuisines, and a highly organised wholesale layer that can give a new supplier national coverage through a single partner.

The decisive structural fact is that almost no foreign supplier sells directly to UK restaurants, pubs or hotels. The market is reached through wholesalers, cash-and-carry operators, buying groups and specialist importers, who act as the UK food business operator and importer of record, handle post-Brexit border formalities and warehousing, and own the sales relationship with the end operator. Choosing the right partner — by channel, product category and country of origin — is therefore the market-entry decision that matters. This study sets out market size and structure, profiles the major players, explains access requirements differentiated by supplier origin, identifies the product groups with the strongest prospects, and provides a working directory of UK importers and distribution partners.
baby-and-toddler-products-austria:
Austria is a small but affluent, high-value market for baby and toddler products. With roughly 9.2 million inhabitants, about 75,000–77,000 births per year and one of the highest purchasing-power levels in the EU, Austrian parents spend significantly above the EU average per child and show a strong preference for quality, safety test results and sustainability. The market is highly integrated with Germany: many retail chains are German-owned and buy centrally in Germany, most international brands serve Austria through their German (DACH) subsidiary or distributor, and German-language product information is mandatory.

Key findings for foreign suppliers:

• Market size: the total Austrian market for baby and toddler products in the Kind + Jugend scope (equipment, furniture, fashion 0–6 years, toys for 0–6 years, care and feeding accessories) is estimated at EUR 1.1–1.4 billion at retail prices. Baby apparel alone accounts for approx. EUR 126 million (2025), children’s apparel overall for approx. EUR 1.2 billion.

• Demographics: births have declined for several years (76,873 in 2024; crude birth rate 8.2 per 1,000 in 2025, total fertility rate 1.29). Volume growth is therefore limited; growth comes from premiumisation, first-time-parent spending, grandparent gifting, tourism (Vienna, alpine regions) and replacement of products after regulatory changes (e.g. i-Size car seats).

• Structure: distribution is concentrated. Drugstores (dm, BIPA, Müller), food retail and discounters (SPAR, REWE/BILLA, HOFER, Lidl), the baby specialist chains (BabyOne, baby-walz), the toy superstore chain Smyths Toys, furniture groups (XXXLutz/Möbelix/mömax, IKEA), value fashion chains and Amazon account for the majority of sales, complemented by a network of independent specialist retailers.

• Importer landscape: there are only a few Austria-based full-range baby importers. Many brands are distributed by German DACH distributors or by the brands’ own subsidiaries. For foreign suppliers, the most realistic routes are (a) direct listing with retail chains that import themselves (private label or brand), (b) Austrian toy and fashion distributors/agencies, and (c) a DACH distributor in Germany that also covers Austria.

• Opportunities: sustainable and organic textiles, wooden and Montessori toys, premium and lightweight travel strollers, e-strollers, reboarder car seats (i-Size), outdoor and alpine family products (bike trailers, child carriers, snow suits, sledges), kids’ traditional wear (Tracht), smart safety products (video monitors), silicone/stainless feeding products and private-label programmes for discounters and drugstores.

• Market access: EU suppliers benefit from free movement of goods but must comply with EU product safety law (GPSR, toy safety, REACH, standards such as EN 71, EN 1888, UN R129), Austrian packaging and WEEE extended producer responsibility and German-language labelling. Non-EU suppliers additionally need an EU-based responsible economic operator, customs clearance (EORI, duties depending on origin and product) and import VAT of 20%.

1. Executive Summary

India is the world's largest birth market, with roughly 23 to 26 million births per year – close to one fifth of all births worldwide. Combined with rising household incomes, nuclear families, dual-income urban parents and fast-growing e-commerce, this makes India one of the most dynamic markets for baby and toddler products. Depending on definition, published estimates put the baby care products market (skin and hair care, toiletries, diapers and wipes, baby food) at USD 4.8–8.4 billion in 2025, with expected annual growth of 9–15%. The toy market adds a further USD 2.1–2.8 billion, and baby equipment, nursery furniture and kidswear come on top. The market is still predominantly mass-market (around 80% of baby care value) and price-sensitive, but a premium segment led by metro cities is expanding quickly. Premium strollers, travel systems, car seats, breast pumps, feeding appliances, smart sleep products and "clean-label" skincare are the most attractive entry points for foreign brands. Private-label and OEM supply to Indian retailers and D2C brands (FirstCry's BabyHug, LuvLap, Mee Mee, R for Rabbit) is the main route for no-name manufacturers. Market access is demanding. India uses mandatory Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) certification for toys, feeding bottles and baby diapers – foreign factories need their own BIS licence – and toys carry a basic customs duty of 70%. Cosmetics require a CDSCO import registration; baby food falls under FSSAI rules and the Infant Milk Substitutes (IMS) Act, which bans promotion of infant formula and feeding bottles. Legal Metrology labelling (importer name, MRP, date of import) applies to all pre-packaged goods. For EU suppliers, the EU–India Free Trade Agreement concluded on 27 January 2026 is the key development: it is expected to be signed around December 2026 and to enter into force in 2027, with tariffs reduced in stages. Until then, standard (MFN) duties apply. EFTA suppliers already benefit from the India–EFTA TEPA, while Korea, Japan, ASEAN, Singapore, the UAE, Australia and Mauritius have their own preferential agreements. The directory in chapter 8 lists the most relevant retailers, importers, distributors and marketplaces with website, general e-mail address and switchboard number where published.
granular-sulphur-bright-yellow-germany:
This study assesses the German market for bright yellow granular (formed) elemental sulphur from the perspective of an Indian manufacturer or exporter planning to enter Germany. It covers demand, buyer groups, importers and distributors, quality requirements, prices, competition, trade flows, distribution structures and market access requirements. Data reflect the situation as of September 2026.

• Germany is a mature, mid-sized and structurally changing sulphur market. Domestic sulphur recovered from sour-gas processing fell from about 1.1 million tonnes in 2000 to about 284,000 tonnes in 2025. Refinery sulphur adds further volumes. Germany is still a net exporter of elemental sulphur (2023: exports of about 220,000 t versus imports of about 60,000 t), but the decline of domestic gas-based output is steadily reducing local supply.

• The addressable import market for solid granular sulphur is niche but real. Large sulphuric acid producers mostly use liquid (molten) sulphur supplied by rail or barge from domestic and Benelux producers. Imported granular sulphur is mainly bought by traders and distributors, fertiliser and agricultural input companies, rubber and chemical processors and smaller acid or SO2 producers with their own melting capacity. Recent import volumes are in the range of 50,000–70,000 t per year.

• 2026 is an extraordinary year for prices. Following the US–Iran conflict and the near-closure of the Strait of Hormuz, Middle East sulphur prices hit all-time records (ADNOC OSP USD 1,000/t fob in July and August 2026, KPC USD 865/t fob in September 2026, compared with about USD 520–530/t fob in February 2026). German delivered prices moved from about USD 750/t to USD 850/t between April and June 2026.

• Critical constraint for an Indian supplier: in July 2026 Indian refiners were effectively barred from exporting sulphur so that domestic fertiliser producers are supplied first. The measure was not formalised in a published decree but is widely applied in the market. Any export project must first confirm, in writing, that the specific material and origin may legally be exported (e.g. confirmation from DGFT/customs broker and the producing refinery).

• Market access is comparatively simple on the customs side (0 % duty for crude/unrefined sulphur CN 2503 00 10; 1.7 % for other sulphur CN 2503 00 90), but REACH registration via an EU Only Representative, a German-language safety data sheet and a reliable certificate of analysis are mandatory in practice. Formed sulphur (granules, prills, pastilles) is exempt from ADR/RID/ADN/IMDG dangerous goods rules under special provision 242.

• Recommendation: enter through two or three established traders/distributors (e.g. Sojitz Solvadis, HELM, Brenntag, Biesterfeld) and selected agricultural repackers, using container shipments in 1 t FIBCs or 25/50 kg bags; position the product as a reliable non-Gulf origin with consistent bright-yellow quality (≥ 99.5 % S, low ash/carbon, low As/Se), and prepare REACH, SDS and origin documentation before the first offer.
baby-and-toddler-products-denmark:
Denmark is a small but affluent, design-conscious and highly digital market for baby and toddler products. With around 6.0 million inhabitants, one of the highest per-capita purchasing powers in the EU and a strong culture of quality, safety and sustainability, it rewards suppliers who combine functional design with verified product safety and credible environmental credentials.

Key facts for foreign suppliers:

• Births are rising again: 59,443 children were born in 2025, 2,364 more than in 2024 (+4.1 %). The total fertility rate rose to 1.506 (2024: 1.466). Statistics Denmark projects around 64,000 births in 2030.

• Estimated market volume for the Kind + Jugend product scope (nursery equipment, furniture, textiles, feeding and care accessories, safety, baby and children's fashion 0–6 years and toys for 0–6 years): approx. DKK 6.8–8.4 billion (EUR 0.9–1.1 billion) at retail prices incl. 25 % VAT (own estimate, see chapter 2).

• Concentrated specialist retail, strong online: BabySam is the leading baby-equipment chain; online specialists (Luksusbaby, Jollyroom, Kids-world, Coolshop) and the Salling Group (Bilka, Føtex, Netto and the BR toy chain) dominate volume. Well-established Danish distributors such as Maki, Scandinavian Baby Products and BabyDan open doors to 1,500+ retail customers.

• Strong domestic brands: Danish design brands (e.g. Konges Sløjd, Liewood, Done by Deer, That's Mine, Sebra, Flexa, Bibs, Hevea, Filibabba) set high standards in design and material quality. Foreign suppliers win with clear differentiation – innovation, certified safety, price-performance or niche specialisation.

• Opportunities exist for both branded products (premium nursery, functional PFAS-free outerwear, natural and educational toys, travel and bike accessories) and no-name/private label (Salling, Coop, Lidl, Rema 1000, BabySam own products, OEM programmes of Danish distributors).

• Market access is EU-harmonised (CE, GPSR, EN standards, REACH) plus Danish specifics: safety information and warnings in Danish, the national PFAS ban for clothing and footwear in force since 1 July 2026, extended producer responsibility for packaging and consumer-driven chemical scrutiny (Forbrugerrådet Tænk, Nordic Swan Ecolabel).

• Recommended entry route: an exclusive Danish or Nordic distributor for hardgoods and toys; an agency for fashion; direct negotiations with BabySam, Salling Group and the online specialists for suppliers with sufficient volume and Danish-language compliance. Denmark is often used as a test market and springboard for Sweden, Norway and Finland.
baby-and-toddler-products-finland:
Finland is a small (5.65 million inhabitants) but affluent, highly organised and quality-driven market for baby and toddler products. After more than a decade of falling birth rates, births have started to recover: according to preliminary THL data, 45,974 children were born in 2025 (+4.8 %), and Statistics Finland reported a further +8.3 % in January–April 2026. The total fertility rate rose from 1.25 to 1.30. For suppliers this means a stable-to-growing customer base after years of contraction, with a pronounced share of first-time parents –the buyers of complete equipment sets.

We estimate the Finnish retail market for the product groups covered by Kind+Jugend (excluding baby food) at roughly EUR 0.55–0.75 billion per year (retail value incl. VAT). Toys and games (approx. EUR 200–230 m) and baby/toddler apparel and footwear (approx. EUR 110–150 m) are the largest blocks, followed by baby care and hygiene, prams and car seats, nursery furniture and feeding/care accessories.

Distribution is concentrated. The two grocery groups S Group (SOK) and K Group (Kesko) together control roughly four-fifths of grocery retail and dominate mass-market toys, baby care and basic children’s clothing through Prisma and K-Citymarket hypermarkets. The discount chain Tokmanni is the price leader in toys and no-name goods. Baby equipment (prams, car seats, nursery) is sold mainly through specialists – above all Lastentarvike Oy, the country’s largest importer and specialist chain – and a group of strong independent specialists and web shops (A-T Lastenturva, Wauva, OZBaby, Ora, Vaunula, Muksumassi) plus the Nordic online leader Jollyroom. Premium toys and design products are channelled through niche importers such as Kiddex and Ketunleikki; mass toys through wholesalers such as Martinex, Toypap and members of the Finnish Toy Association.

Best opportunities exist for products that solve Nordic-specific needs (winter-proof prams and accessories, footmuffs, thermal and outdoor clothing, reflective safety items, rear-facing car seats), for demonstrably sustainable and non-toxic products (organic textiles, natural rubber, FSC wood, recycled materials), for compact and multifunctional products for urban flats, for development-oriented and Montessori-style toys, and for private-label programmes for S Group, K Group, Tokmanni, Jollyroom and importers’ own brands. The public day-care sector and the annual Kela maternity package tender are additional B2B channels.

Market access is governed by EU law: EU suppliers benefit from free movement of goods and only need to meet product-safety, chemical, labelling (Finnish and Swedish) and producer-responsibility rules. Suppliers from non-EU Europe additionally face customs formalities, but often duty-free access under free-trade agreements. Extra-European suppliers must also clear customs, pay duties per the EU tariff, appoint an EU-based responsible economic operator and usually provide social-compliance audits. Since 1 July 2026, low-value e-commerce parcels from outside the EU are subject to a flat EUR 3 customs duty per item.

Chapter 7 contains a directory of 39 Finnish (and Nordic) importers, distributors, direct-importing retailers and institutional channels, each with website and, where published, a general e-mail address, switchboard number and supplier-registration link.

1. Executive Summary

South Korea is a small but exceptionally valuable market for baby and toddler products. After eight consecutive years of decline, births have rebounded: 254,300 babies were born in 2025 (+6.7 % year on year, the highest number since 2021) and the total fertility rate rose to 0.80, the second annual increase in a row. Marriages - the leading indicator for births - grew by 14.8 % in 2024 and by a further 8.1 % in 2025, which points to continued demand in 2026 and 2027. What makes Korea attractive for foreign suppliers is not volume but value per child. Most families have only one child, mothers are older (average age at birth 33.8 years; 37 % of births to mothers aged 35+) and household spending is supported by generous state cash benefits (KRW 1 million per month in the first year of life). Parents and grandparents concentrate their spending on premium, safety-certified and design-led products, and European brands enjoy an outstanding reputation - Stokke, Bugaboo, Cybex, Joie, BabyBjörn and Ergobaby are household names. Market research estimates the Korean baby products market (excluding food) at roughly USD 3.4 billion in 2025, growing at around 5.8 % p.a. to about USD 5.3 billion by 2033. Baby cosmetics & toiletries is the largest segment; feeding & nursing is the fastest growing. Disposable diapers alone account for about USD 1.6 billion, and baby food & infant nutrition for a further ~USD 1.3 billion. The wider "kids industry" (including education, services and apparel) is estimated at around KRW 60 trillion. Market access is regulated but transparent. Every children's product (up to age 13) must carry a Korean KC mark under the Special Act on the Safety of Children's Products, issued through one of three procedures (safety certification, safety confirmation or supplier's declaration of conformity) and generally held by the Korean importer. Feeding utensils, baby food, baby cosmetics, wipes and diapers fall under the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety (MFDS). The FTA network determines the tariff: EU, UK, EFTA, Turkish, US, ASEAN, Australian and Canadian goods generally enter duty-free, whereas suppliers without a free trade agreement pay MFN duties of typically 5 % (strollers), 8 % (toys) or 13 % (apparel), plus 10 % VAT for everyone. Distribution is highly concentrated online (Coupang, Naver, SSG/E-Mart, Lotte ON) and in a small number of experienced import distributors that hold exclusive brand rights, build KC certification, run after-sales service and warranty registration, and sell across online, department stores, hypermarkets and the large consumer baby fairs. The recommended route for most newcomers is therefore an exclusive or category-exclusive distribution agreement with a specialised Korean importer, complemented by private-label or OEM supply to retailers (E-Mart "No Brand", Coupang private label, Daiso) for no-name products. Chapter 9 provides a classified directory of relevant importers, distributors and directly importing retailers with website, general e-mail, switchboard and supplier-registration links.

1. Executive Summary

China remains one of the largest markets in the world for baby, toddler and children’s products, even though the number of births has fallen sharply. The National Bureau of Statistics recorded 7.92 million births in 2025, 17% fewer than the 9.54 million of 2024 and the lowest figure since records began in 1949. Despite this, spending continues to grow because parents spend considerably more per child, buy more premium products and increasingly shop online. According to Frost & Sullivan data published in a June 2026 Hong Kong listing document, China’s maternal, infant and child products and services market reached a gross merchandise value (GMV) of RMB 4,124 billion in 2025 (approx. USD 573 billion), of which RMB 3,214 billion were products. The non-food product segment, which covers the Kind + Jugend categories (equipment, durables, textiles, toys, care and consumables), grew from RMB 838 billion in 2020 to RMB 1,035 billion in 2025 (approx. USD 144 billion / EUR 125 billion) and is forecast to reach RMB 1,187 billion by 2029. The market is extremely fragmented: even the leading specialist retailer Kidswant reaches only about 0.3% market share, and the five largest players together account for roughly 1%. For foreign suppliers this is both an opportunity and a challenge – there is no single gatekeeper, but success requires a well-chosen partner mix of specialist chains, national distributors and online platforms. Key findings for foreign suppliers: • Premiumisation instead of volume: annual spending per child aged 0–3 reached around RMB 48,000 in 2025 and is expected to rise to about RMB 72,000 by 2030. Safety, science-based claims, design and materials quality drive purchasing decisions. • Online is the main battleground: the online share of maternity and baby sales rose from 35.1% (2023) to 46.1% (2025). Tmall, JD.com, Douyin and Xiaohongshu are essential for visibility, but specialist chains remain important for advice-intensive products (car seats, strollers, nursery). • Policy tailwind: since 2025 a national childcare subsidy of RMB 3,600 per year is paid for every child under three, which particularly lifts purchasing power in lower-tier cities. • Two entry routes: cross-border e-commerce (CBEC) allows market testing without CCC certification or Chinese labelling within consumer limits; general trade requires CCC for regulated products (toys, strollers, walkers, children’s bicycles, car seats) and compliance with mandatory GB standards. • Regulatory change 2026/2027: new toy safety standards (GB 6675-2025 series) and new general safety standards for children’s products and child care articles take effect on 1 November 2026; revised CCC rules for toys and children’s vehicles apply to new certifications from that date, with a transition period until 30 November 2027. • Branded vs. no-name: foreign brands with a clear safety, design or origin story (“European safety”, “Japanese quality”) have the best chances. Pure no-name products struggle against China’s domestic manufacturing base; realistic opportunities exist in premium niches, specialised materials and components, and in cross-border “global selection” ranges of retailers and platforms. • Supplier origin matters: EU suppliers pay MFN duties (no EU–China FTA); suppliers from Switzerland, Iceland, Serbia and Georgia and from RCEP countries (Japan, Korea, ASEAN, Australia, New Zealand) can benefit from preferential tariffs; US-origin goods currently face an additional 10% Chinese retaliatory tariff.
baby-and-toddler-products-france:
France is one of the three largest European markets for baby, toddler and children’s products. Although the birth rate is falling – 643,905 births in 2025, around 24% fewer than at the 2010 peak, with a fertility rate of 1.56 children per woman – spending per child is rising, parents are older (average age at birth 31.2 years) and grandparents play an important role as buyers. The result is a value-driven market in which premium, safe, durable and sustainable products gain share while volume declines.

The relevant market (the product scope shown at trade fairs such as Kind+Jugend in Cologne) can be broken down into four blocks: (1) baby equipment or “puériculture” – strollers, car seats, nursery furniture, feeding, bathing, sleep and safety products – estimated at around EUR 850 million; (2) the wider “baby markets” including textiles, infant nutrition, hygiene and early-age toys, which Circana puts at around EUR 2.85 billion; (3) the toys and games market, which reached a record EUR 4.7 billion in 2025 (+7.1%); and (4) children’s and baby fashion, a multi-billion-euro segment dominated by French chains and own brands.

Distribution is concentrated. Specialist chains (Aubert, Bébé 9, Autour de Bébé, Orchestra, Vertbaudet) account for roughly two thirds of puériculture sales; children’s fashion is dominated by French specialist chains (Kiabi, Okaïdi/IDKIDS, Tape à l’œil, Sergent Major, DPAM, Jacadi, Petit Bateau); toys are sold through specialist chains (King Jouet, JouéClub, La Grande Récré, Picwic, Smyths), hypermarkets and online. Discounters (Action, Gifi, B&M, Stokomani, Lidl, Aldi) are important buyers of no-name and private-label products.

For foreign suppliers the best entry routes are: (a) a French or Benelux-based distributor/brand house that already serves the specialist channel (for branded, innovative hard goods), (b) direct listing with a specialist chain or its buying cooperative, (c) private-label and own-brand programmes of retailers and discounters (for no-name suppliers), and (d) marketplaces (Amazon, Cdiscount, Vertbaudet, Aubert) to test demand. Market access is governed by EU harmonised product-safety law (GPSR, Toy Safety Directive/Regulation, EN standards, REACH), complemented by specific French rules: French-language labelling, the French decree on childcare articles, extended producer responsibility (EPR/“REP”) registration with a unique identifier, Triman/Info-tri marking and –for textiles – the new anti-ultra-fast-fashion law of July 2026.
baby-and-toddler-products-italy:
Italy is Europe’s fourth-largest market for nursery products and one of the most brand- and design-conscious baby markets in the world. At the same time it is a market under demographic pressure: births fell to about 370,000 in 2024 and to a new historic low of roughly 355,000 in 2025, with a fertility rate of only about 1.14 children per woman. Fewer babies, older and wealthier first-time parents and strong involvement of grandparents translate into a market that is shrinking in units but where spending per child remains high and consumers trade up to safe, well-designed and durable products.

For the core scope of this study (nursery equipment, furniture and textiles, 0–3 apparel and infant/pre-school toys) we estimate a retail value of roughly €1.8–2.2 billion. Including the FMCG baby categories (nappies, wipes, toiletries and baby food), the total mother-and-baby market exceeds €4 billion. The nursery segment tracked by NIQ declined by about 3% in value in 2025, while car seats (driven by stricter rules) and baby electronics grew.

Key findings for foreign suppliers:

• Concentrated retail, fragmented specialists: Prénatal Retail Group (Prénatal, Toys Center, Bimbostore) dominates specialist retail; the rest of the specialist channel is organised in buying groups and consortia (GIPI, Io Bimbo, Beberoyal) and several hundred independent stores, which are served by importers and agents.

• Strong domestic brands: Chicco (Artsana), Peg Perego, Inglesina, Foppapedretti, Brevi, Cam, Picci and Pali set high expectations for quality and design in heavy nursery and furniture. New entrants succeed with clear differentiation – innovation, safety features, sustainability or price-performance.

• Best opportunities: i-Size (R129) car seats and anti-abandonment devices, compact travel strollers, baby electronics (monitors, bottle preparers, sterilisers, breast pumps), convertible/evolving furniture, sleep products, ergonomic carriers, silicone and sustainable feeding ranges, Montessori-style wooden toys and ceremonial/gift clothing.

• Private label: grocery chains, discounters (Lidl, Eurospin), non-food discounters (Action, Pepco), apparel chains (OVS, Original Marines, Piazza Italia) and the specialist groups’ own labels offer volume business for no-name manufacturers with robust compliance and test documentation.

• Market access: EU suppliers benefit from free movement of goods; all suppliers must comply with the General Product Safety Regulation, toy and childcare standards and Italy-specific labelling rules (Italian language, environmental packaging labels, EPR registrations). Non-EU suppliers additionally need an EU-based economic operator, customs clearance and must factor in duties (e.g. about 12% for apparel) and 22% VAT. Section 8 lists importers, distributors, buying groups and directly importing retailers with website and – where published – general e-mail, switchboard number and supplier registration links, grouped by channel and product focus.
baby-and-toddler-products-netherlands:
The Netherlands is a compact, affluent and highly digital market of about 18 million inhabitants with roughly 166,000 births per year. It is small in birth numbers compared with Germany or France, but it combines high purchasing power per child, a strong preference for design and quality, very high online shopping penetration and one of the most efficient logistics infrastructures in Europe (Rotterdam, Schiphol, dense distribution-centre network). For foreign suppliers it is also a natural test market and a gateway to the Benelux and, via Dutch distributors with DACH coverage, to the German-speaking markets.

Market volume. Based on birth cohorts, typical per-child spending and retailer turnover, the core baby and toddler non-food market (0–3 years: nursery hardgoods, furniture, textiles, apparel and shoes, baby and toddler toys, care and feeding accessories) is estimated at approximately EUR 1.1–1.4 billion at retail prices (incl. VAT). Adjacent consumables – baby food (around USD 1.2 billion) and baby-specific personal care –add a further large volume but are outside the core scope of this study.

Market structure. Specialised baby superstores (Babypark/Baby-Dump, Prénatal, Van Asten, BabyPlanet), generalist discounters and variety chains (Action, HEMA, Zeeman, Wibra, Kruidvat, Xenos), fashion retailers and a very strong online segment (bol, Amazon.nl, specialist webshops) share the market. Dutch brand houses such as Bugaboo, Joolz, Mutsy, Easywalker, Maxi-Cosi, Nuna, Jollein, Little Dutch, Bopita and Kidsmill are internationally visible, which makes the domestic market demanding but also receptive to well-designed innovations.

Opportunities. The best chances for new foreign suppliers lie in (1) innovative, design-led hardgoods and smart products introduced via specialist distributors, (2) sustainable textiles and sleep products, (3) products tailored to Dutch living conditions – cycling, small homes, steep stairs, rain – and (4) competitively priced private-label ranges for discounters, drugstores and variety chains. No-name suppliers should target retail own-brands and importers of general merchandise; branded suppliers should appoint a Benelux distributor or agency with access to the specialist chains and marketplaces.

Market access. EU suppliers benefit from free movement of goods but must comply with EU product safety law (GPSR, harmonised EN standards, Toy Safety Directive – and from 1 August 2030 the new Toy Safety Regulation), REACH, textile labelling, Dutch-language instructions and Dutch extended producer responsibility schemes (textiles, packaging, electronics/batteries). Non-EU European and non-European suppliers additionally need customs clearance, an EU-based economic operator responsible for product compliance, correct origin documentation and must budget for import duties that are notably high for apparel and home textiles.

Directory. Section 9 lists more than 60 relevant Dutch importers, distributors, agencies, direct-importing retailers and platforms, grouped by baby specialists versus generalists and by type (full-range, category specialist, direct-importing retailer, marketplace). For each entry the website is given, plus – where publicly available – the general e-mail address, the switchboard number and links to supplier information or registration pages.
baby-and-toddler-products-norway:
Norway is a small but exceptionally affluent market for baby and toddler products. With about 55,400 births in 2025 and one of the highest purchasing powers in Europe, Norwegian parents spend well above the European average per child, favour quality, safety and functional Scandinavian design, and are willing to pay for products that cope with long winters, outdoor naps and an active outdoor lifestyle. After more than a decade of decline, births have now risen for three consecutive years.

The total market for baby and toddler products covered by the Kind+Jugend product spectrum (nursery equipment, prams and car seats, furniture, textiles, feeding and care accessories, clothing, toys, plus diapers, toiletries and baby food) is estimated at roughly NOK 8–10 billion (approx. EUR 0.7–0.9 billion) at retail value. Distribution is concentrated: one specialist chain (Barnas Hus) dominates the bricks-and-mortar specialist trade, Swedish-based Jollyroom leads online, three grocery groups control FMCG baby care, and a handful of toy chains and distributors dominate toys.

Key findings for foreign suppliers:

• Norway is in the EEA but not in the EU customs union. EU product rules (CE, toy safety, REACH, cosmetics) apply, but every shipment – even from Germany or Sweden – is an import with customs declaration and 25% VAT. Industrial goods are duty-free; clothing and textiles are the main exception and depend on proof of preferential origin.

• Distributor model is the norm. Most brands enter via a Norwegian or Nordic distributor who serves specialist chains, independents, kindergartens and online retailers; only the largest chains buy directly from foreign manufacturers.

• Best opportunities lie in winter/outdoor products (pram sleeping bags, wool and outdoor clothing, all-terrain prams), rear-facing car-seat accessories, sustainable wooden and Montessori toys, silicone/feeding products, sleep and monitoring products, and private label for chains and discounters.

• Compliance and ethics are gatekeepers. Buyers expect full EN/CE documentation, chemical compliance (PFAS, phthalates), Norwegian-language safety information and evidence of responsible sourcing under Norway's Transparency Act.

1. Executive Summary

Singapore is a small but affluent, highly import-dependent market for baby and toddler products. With roughly 30,000 live births a year, 6.2 million inhabitants and one of the highest per-capita incomes in Asia, the market rewards quality, safety, design and convenience rather than volume. Practically all non-food baby and toddler products are imported, and the country charges no customs duty on them – only the 9% Goods and Services Tax (GST) at import. Market volume. Based on published segment data, the core baby and toddler market (baby food, baby and toddler apparel, toys for toddlers and young children, baby safety products, baby toiletries) is worth roughly EUR 370 million a year. Including nappies and wipes, strollers and car seats, nursery furniture, feeding accessories and maternity products, the total addressable market for the categories covered in this study is estimated at EUR 550–700 million (approx. SGD 0.8–1.0 billion) at retail prices. The overall toys and games market (including video games) reached SGD 1.23 billion in 2025. Structure. Distribution is concentrated: a handful of specialist chains (Mothercare, Kiddy Palace, Motherswork, Toys"R"Us/Babies"R"Us), Japanese and local department stores (Takashimaya, Isetan, OG, BHG, Mustafa), grocery and drugstore chains (FairPrice, DFI Retail Group with CS Fresh/Giant/Guardian, Sheng Siong, Watsons) and the marketplaces Shopee, Lazada and Amazon.sg. Several of the leading specialist retailers are also exclusive importers and distributors for dozens of brands, which makes them the natural first contacts for foreign suppliers. Opportunities. Falling birth numbers (resident total fertility rate 0.87 in 2025) are offset by premiumisation, high spending per child, multiple gift-givers per child (parents, grandparents, relatives) and strong government baby support. The best prospects are premium and design-led nursery and travel gear, space-saving and multi-stage products suited to compact high-rise flats, certified-safe car seats and sleep products, feeding and breast-pump innovations, natural/organic skincare, sustainable textiles, and educational, wooden and STEM toys. Private label is relevant for retailer house brands (FairPrice, Watsons, Guardian, Mothercare group) and for importers that build their own brands. Market access. There is no pre-market approval for most non-food baby products. General consumer goods – toys, childcare articles, furniture, textiles – must meet at least one recognised international, regional or national safety standard under the Consumer Goods Safety Requirements Regulations (CGSR), and authorities run active post-market surveillance. Separate regimes apply to infant formula and baby food (Singapore Food Agency), baby cosmetics (Health Sciences Authority notification), certain electrical appliances (SAFETY Mark), wireless devices such as baby monitors (IMDA) and child car seats (recognised vehicle-restraint standards). Origin. Because Singapore applies zero duty to these goods, the supplier's origin rarely matters for import costs. It matters for standards documentation (EN, ASTM, ISO and AS/NZS reports are all accepted), consumer perception (European, Japanese and Korean brands command premium prices) and logistics. EU suppliers benefit from the EU–Singapore Free Trade Agreement and familiarity with EN standards; non-EU European suppliers from the UK and EFTA agreements; non-European suppliers mainly from close regional logistics and, in the case of the US, Japan, Korea and Australia, strong brand recognition. Directory. Chapter 9 lists 30 importers, distributors, retailers that import directly and marketplaces, classified as specialist importers, specialist retailers, full-range/generalist importers and large retailers, and online platforms, with website, general e-mail address and central telephone number where publicly available and links to supplier registration pages where they exist.
fmcg-market-germany:
Germany is the largest consumer market in the European Union: around 84 million inhabitants and private consumption of some €2,200 billion in 2024, of which around 30 percent — some €664 billion — flows through retail. Food retail reached €270.8 billion in 2024 on a broad definition, 3.8 percent more than the previous year; the drugstore trade reached around €23 billion across some 5,100 stores and is the fastest-growing part of German FMCG retail as well as the decisive channel for non-food.

FMCG goods live on rotation, not on margin per unit. The margin per unit is thin, the purchase decision is made in seconds at the shelf, and availability is decisive: a product that is missing is not bought later, but replaced — and repeated substitution ends a listing. This study covers both halves of the sector, food and non-food, which in German retail practice are often bought by the same trading houses and sold through the same channels. It sets out market volume and channel structure, names the leading players, explains the access requirements for suppliers from the EU, from non-EU Europe and from outside Europe, and contains a directory of German FMCG importers and distributors.
baby-and-toddler-products-poland:
Poland is the largest consumer market in Central and Eastern Europe (37.3 million inhabitants) and a structurally attractive, although demographically challenged, market for baby and toddler products. Births fell to about 238,000 in 2025 – the lowest level since 1945 and more than 40 % below 2017 – yet spending on children keeps rising. According to OC&C Strategy Consultants, sales of toys, clothing and other children's products reached around PLN 15 bn (≈ EUR 3.5 bn) in 2024 and are expected to exceed PLN 17 bn by 2029.

The market is driven by "fewer children, more spending per child": rising real incomes, generous family transfers (800+ child benefit, the 'Babciowe' / Aktywny Rodzic childcare benefit) and premiumisation. Average annual spending per child was about EUR 540 in 2024, forecast to exceed EUR 680 by 2029 – still well below the UK (EUR 1,280), Italy (EUR 950) or Spain (EUR 830). This gap is the core growth argument for foreign brands with a clear quality or design edge.

Key findings for foreign suppliers:

• Structure: a strong domestic brand layer (Canpol babies, LOVI, BabyOno, Kinderkraft, Lionelo, Caretero, Espiro etc.) competes on value; international premium brands (Cybex, Britax Römer, Maxi-Cosi, Chicco, Philips Avent, LEGO) dominate the upper segments. The space in between – well-designed mid-premium products with a clear functional benefit – is where new entrants find distributors most willingly.

• Channels: e-commerce is the largest single channel (≈ one third of sales; Allegro is the dominant marketplace), followed by specialist chains (Smyk), independent baby stores supplied by wholesalers, drugstores (Rossmann, Hebe, Super-Pharm), discounters (Pepco, Action, Biedronka, Lidl) and hypermarkets.

• Route to market: most foreign brands enter through an exclusive or category-exclusive Polish distributor (e.g. AICO, Marini, IKS 2, Baby & Travel, Angre, Stokkids; for toys Artyk, TM Toys, Brimarex, Dante, EPEE). Private-label opportunities exist with Pepco, Smyk, Rossmann, the discounters and Polish brand owners that source from abroad (4Kraft, BrandLine, IKS 2).

• Hub function: several Polish distributors also serve Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary, Romania and the Baltic states – a Polish partner can open a CEE region of ~70 million consumers.

• Compliance: EU product safety law (GPSR, Toy Safety Directive/EN 71, UN R129 for car seats, EN standards for childcare articles), Polish-language labelling and EPR registration (BDO) are prerequisites. Non-EU suppliers additionally need an EU-based importer/responsible person and face customs duties; since 1 July 2026 a flat EUR 3 duty per item applies to low-value B2C parcels.
fmcg-market-ireland:
Ireland is a compact market in which a small number of retail groups and wholesale operators reach most of the country, so a single well-chosen listing can carry a product nationwide. That concentration is the market's main attraction for a foreign supplier, and also its main barrier: shelf space is contested, own-brand penetration is high, and the buyer's requirements on provenance, packaging and supply reliability are strict.

This study sets out the fast-moving consumer goods landscape across food and non-food, measures market size and channel structure, profiles the leading grocery retailers, wholesalers and buying groups, explains the access requirements for suppliers from the EU, from non-EU Europe and from outside Europe, and provides a directory of Irish FMCG importers and distributors.
fmcg-market-italy:
Italy is one of the largest consumer goods markets in Europe, but also one of the most fragmented: alongside the large national groups and buying centres, organised distribution coexists with a dense network of regional banners and independent shops served by cash & carry and traditional wholesalers. For a foreign supplier this means that the right channel changes from region to region and that the choice of distribution partner matters more than the list price.

This study defines the scope of consumer goods, analyses the food and non-food market, identifies the leading players in modern retail and wholesale, explains the access requirements according to the supplier's origin, and brings together a directory of Italian importers and distributors.
baby-and-toddler-products-portugal:
Portugal is a compact but well-structured market of around 10.7 million inhabitants in which baby and toddler products are sold through a small number of powerful retail groups, a network of Iberian distributors and a lively independent and online specialist scene. After years of decline, the birth rate is recovering: according to the national statistics institute INE, 87,732 babies were born in 2025, 3.3% more than in 2024, and every month except January and February 2025 was above the previous year. Roughly one third of newborns have mothers born abroad, and almost one in three births is to a mother aged 35 or older, which supports demand for well-researched, safety-oriented and premium products.

Taking all Kind+Jugend categories together (nursery hardgoods such as prams, car seats and furniture, light nursery articles for feeding, care and safety, baby and toddler textiles and fashion, and infant and pre-school toys), the core market is estimated at EUR 250–350 million at retail prices. Including the total toy market (all ages) and baby consumables such as diapers, baby personal care and baby food, the addressable children’s economy reaches roughly EUR 0.85–1.0 billion. The toy market grew strongly in early 2025 (+15.1% in value to the end of April according to GfK data), and online toy sales keep gaining share.

The market is shaped by the Sonae group (Continente hypermarkets and the Zippy children’s chain), Jerónimo Martins (Pingo Doce), Auchan, Lidl, El Corte Inglés, the Prénatal Retail Group (which also operates Toys “R” Us in Portugal), the electronics chain Worten and the pharmacy channel. On the supply side, brand subsidiaries such as Artsana (Chicco) coexist with Portuguese toy distributors such as Concentra and Dream Toys and with Spain-based Iberian distributors that manage many international nursery brands for Spain and Portugal from one hub.

For foreign suppliers, the most promising entry routes are (1) an exclusive Portuguese or Iberian distributor for branded ranges, (2) direct listings with large retailers for private-label and value ranges, and (3) Portuguese-language e-commerce and specialist retailers for niche and premium brands. Products with particularly good prospects include i-Size car seats and compact travel systems, co-sleeping and space-saving nursery furniture, sun and heat protection products, sustainable feeding and care articles, baby monitors and smart safety devices, Montessori, wooden and STEM toys, outdoor and ride-on toys and affordable, well-designed private-label basics.

Suppliers from other EU member states benefit from the single market but must still meet the General Product Safety Regulation, the Toy Safety Directive, the relevant EN standards, Portuguese-language labelling and national extended producer responsibility rules. Suppliers from outside the EU additionally need an EU-based responsible economic operator, customs clearance and, for goods sold directly to consumers, must take into account that the EUR 150 duty exemption for low-value parcels was abolished on 1 July 2026.

baby-and-toddler-products-sweden:
Sweden is a small but highly attractive market for baby and toddler products: purchasing power is high, parents are well informed and safety-conscious, both parents take extensive parental leave, and Scandinavian design, sustainability and functionality are decisive purchase criteria. At the same time the market is mature and consolidating. With around 97,500 births in 2025 – the lowest figure in 23 years – volume growth has to come from value (premium, safety, sustainability) and from market-share gains rather than from demographics.

We estimate the Swedish retail market for the product scope of Kind + Jugend (nursery equipment, furniture and textiles, baby and toddler fashion 0–6 years, safety, feeding and care non-food, and toys for 0–6 years) at roughly SEK 14–16 billion (approx. EUR 1.3–1.45 billion) per year at retail prices. Online penetration is among the highest in Europe; the online pure player Jollyroom is the Nordic category leader, while omnichannel specialists (BabySam, Babyproffsen, Bonti, BabyV), the Lekia/Babya store network, pharmacies, grocery chains and variety discounters (Gekås Ullared, Rusta, Clas Ohlson) cover the rest of the market.

For new foreign suppliers the most promising entry routes are: (1) a Nordic distributor or agency that already supplies the specialist trade (e.g. ReiRei, 4P, BabyNord, SBA Baby, GBAB, Pro Support, Leklyckan, Micki), (2) direct listing with online and omnichannel specialists that import directly (Jollyroom, BabySam, Babyshop, Babyland, Lekia/Babya) and (3) private-label manufacturing for retailers with own brands (Jollyroom, pharmacies, grocery and variety retailers, children’s fashion chains).

Categories with particularly good prospects include rear-facing car seats and accessories, all-weather strollers and winter accessories, merino/wool and weatherproof outerwear, ergonomic carriers, sleep and safety products (including connected monitors), sustainable feeding products, perfume-free baby care, open-ended wooden and Montessori-style toys, and child accessories for cargo bikes and e-bikes. Market access is governed by EU harmonised product legislation; non-EU suppliers additionally need an EU-based responsible economic operator, customs clearance and must budget for 25 % import VAT and category-specific duties.

1. About this study

This study is written for manufacturers and suppliers based outside Australia who already sell successfully in their home market and are looking to introduce their brands or products to Australia. It focuses on the whole fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) sector — both food and non-food — and on the single most practical route to market for a new overseas supplier: the Australian FMCG importer and distributor. Importers and distributors matter to foreign suppliers because they already hold the relationships and the logistics that a newcomer lacks. They have direct trading terms with the large supermarket chains and with the wholesale and foodservice trade, they understand Australian import, food-safety and labelling rules, and they can introduce new brands and products in commercially meaningful volumes — whether under the supplier's own brand or as a private (retailer) label. Approaching them first is almost always faster, cheaper and lower-risk than trying to open a supermarket account directly from abroad. The report covers: what FMCG means; the size and structure of the Australian market; the major retail players; the opportunities for new foreign suppliers of branded and unbranded products; the products and categories with the strongest sales potential; and the market-access requirements, distinguishing between suppliers from the European Union, suppliers from non-EU European countries, and suppliers from outside Europe. It closes with a directory of relevant importers and distributors, organised so that a supplier can quickly identify the right type of partner for its products.

2. What is FMCG (Fast-Moving Consumer Goods)?

Fast-moving consumer goods — FMCG, also called consumer packaged goods (CPG) — are inexpensive products that households buy frequently and use up quickly, and that therefore move rapidly off retail shelves. They are characterised by high sales volumes, relatively low unit prices, short repurchase cycles, thin per-unit margins earned back through scale, and wide distribution through supermarkets, convenience stores, pharmacies, discounters and, increasingly, online. FMCG is not only food. The sector is conventionally split into food and non-food, and this study treats both: • Food and beverages — packaged and ambient groceries (pasta, rice, sauces, canned goods, snacks, confectionery, biscuits, breakfast cereals, coffee and tea), chilled and frozen foods, dairy, and drinks (soft drinks, water, juices, and other beverages). • Personal care and cosmetics — skincare, haircare, colour cosmetics, oral care, fragrances and toiletries. • Consumer health / OTC (non-prescription) — vitamins, dietary supplements and everyday self-care products (this study does not deal with prescription medicines). • Household and cleaning — laundry and dishwashing products, surface cleaners, paper goods, kitchen wraps and foils, and other household consumables. • Pet care — pet food, treats, grooming and accessories, one of the most resilient FMCG categories. Two commercial models run through the whole sector. Under the branded model the manufacturer's own brand appears on shelf; under the private-label (or "home brand") model the product is sold under the retailer's or importer's brand. Many Australian importers work in both models at once, and this study flags which partners lean towards building new brands and which are primarily private-label and established-brand distributors

3. Market size and structure

Australia is a wealthy, stable and highly urbanised consumer market of roughly 27.7 million people (September 2025), with high disposable incomes and consumer spending that has proven resilient through economic cycles. Population growth, driven largely by net overseas migration, continues to expand the customer base and is one of the structural drivers of grocery demand. Market-size figures vary by definition and source. The core supermarket and grocery-store retail market is estimated at roughly AUD 140–150 billion a year, while broader estimates of the total FMCG sector (adding non-food categories and other channels) reach around AUD 165–170 billion. However it is measured, food and Page 3 The Australian FMCG Market — Market Entry Study beverages make up the large majority of value — of the order of 70 per cent — with non-food FMCG making up the balance.
