1. Executive Summary

Serbia (6.6 million inhabitants) is the largest food and beverage market of the Western Balkans and the logistics hub for the wider ex-Yugoslav region. Its HoReCa (hotels, restaurants, cafés/catering) sector is fragmented, price-sensitive and concentrated in Belgrade and Novi Sad, but it is modernising quickly: restaurant chains, international hotel brands and delivery platforms are expanding, while a persistent shortage of kitchen staff is driving demand for convenience, frozen and semi-prepared products. Key findings for foreign suppliers:  Market size: Revenue of restaurants and takeaways is estimated at around EUR 3.7 billion for 2026; food and drink wholesaling at around EUR 10.6 billion. In 2025 Serbia recorded 4.35 million tourist arrivals (2.35 million foreign) and 12.3 million overnight stays.  Growth catalyst: Expo 2027 Belgrade (15 May – 15 August 2027) is expected by the organiser to attract more than four million visitors, with more than 120 participating countries, and is triggering investment in hotels and food outlets.  Route to market: Supply runs through three channels: Cash & Carry (METRO is the only nationwide operator, plus Mercator-S Velpro), national FMCG distributors serving both retail and HoReCa (Nelt, Delta DMD, Atlantic Grupa), and specialised HoReCa importers (Corp JVJV, SCB, M&L International and category specialists). Foreign brands nearly always enter through such a local importer.  Best opportunities: Frozen convenience (potato products, bakery, desserts), Italian and world-cuisine ingredients, premium coffee and tea, mineral water and mixers, fish and seafood, plant-based and "posno" (Orthodox fasting) products, gluten-free lines and pastry/bakery ingredients. Private label is relevant mainly through METRO and the retail chains.  Access: Serbia is an EU candidate country and has largely harmonised its food law with the EU (labelling in line with Regulation (EU) 1169/2011). Products must carry a Serbian-language label (stickering permitted) naming the Serbian importer. Products of animal origin require prior import approval from the Veterinary Directorate. EU, CEFTA, EFTA, UK, Turkish and EAEU suppliers benefit from free-trade agreements; since July 2024 also China. Other origins pay MFN duties of 0–30 % on agricultural products. Serbia is not a WTO member.
horeca-foodservice-market-venezuela:
Venezuela's food and beverage market was estimated at around USD 1,080 million in 2025, with projections pointing to some USD 1,900 million by 2032, at a high single-digit compound growth rate. It is a small market by value and an atypical one in how it works: the de facto dollarisation of a large part of transactions has substantially changed purchasing conditions compared with the previous decade.

For a foreign supplier, that means the older market references describe a country that no longer exists commercially, and that the choice of importer — for its access to foreign currency, its logistics and its customer base — matters more than in any other market in the region. This study sets out the structure of the market and its channels, the access and import requirements according to the supplier's origin and the categories with the best prospects, and includes a directory of Venezuelan importers and distributors in the HoReCa channel.
baby-and-toddler-products-spain:
Spain is Europe's fourth-largest consumer market for baby and toddler products and a gateway to the Iberian Peninsula. Structurally, the market is shaped by one of the lowest fertility rates in the EU (1.10 children per woman) but a stable base of around 320,000 births per year – in 2025 births rose by 1.0 % to 321,164, the first increase in a decade. Fewer children, older and better-educated parents and a high share of first-born children translate into higher spending per child, a clear trend towards premium, safety-certified and design-oriented products, and a strong gifting culture (grandparents, baby showers, christenings).

We estimate the retail value of the product universe presented at trade fairs such as Kind+Jugend (nursery hardgoods, furniture, sleep and textiles, feeding and care, safety, first-age toys and baby/toddler fashion) at roughly €1.7–2.2 billion per year, plus about €0.4 billion for nappies and wipes. The Spanish manufacturing side (fashion, footwear and nursery goods) invoiced €1.134 billion in 2024, more than half of it exported, while the total toy sector reached about €1.5 billion; both segments returned to modest growth in 2025.

Distribution is concentrated in a handful of gatekeepers: specialist Iberian importer-distributors (who typically hold exclusive rights for Spain and Portugal), El Corte Inglés, the Prénatal Retail Group (Toys "R" Us and Prénatal), Amazon, the hypermarket chains, pharmacies for feeding and care, and toy buying groups. Independent specialist stores still matter for strollers and car seats but are shrinking. For most foreign suppliers the fastest and lowest-risk route is an exclusive Iberian distributor, complemented by Amazon for visibility; private-label manufacturers should target discounters, hypermarkets and fashion chains directly.

Best prospects exist for lightweight/compact travel strollers, i-Size car seats (especially extended rear-facing), bedside co-sleeping cribs and convertible furniture for small urban flats, premium feeding and breastfeeding products, connected monitoring (subject to the new EU radio-equipment cybersecurity rules), sun-protection and hot-climate products, organic textiles and sleeping bags, Montessori/wooden and educational toys, and value private-label consumables and accessories.

Market access is governed by harmonised EU law. EU suppliers enjoy free movement but must still register for Spanish extended producer responsibility (packaging, electrical equipment, batteries) and label in Spanish. Suppliers from non-EU Europe (UK, Switzerland, Norway, Turkey) can usually import duty-free under preferential agreements but face customs formalities. Suppliers from outside Europe pay customs duties of 0–12 % depending on the product, 21 % import VAT and need an EU-based economic operator; import consignments of toys and childcare articles may be subject to SOIVRE product-safety inspection.

Section 8 lists 52 relevant Spanish importers, distributors and directly importing retailers, separated into baby and toddler specialists and non-food companies that handle baby products or toys as one category among others.
baby-and-toddler-products-switzerland:
Switzerland is a small but exceptionally valuable market for baby and toddler products. With 9.13 million inhabitants at the end of 2025 and around 78,200 births per year, it offers one of the highest per-child spending levels in Europe, a strong preference for quality, safety and design, and a retail structure that is concentrated enough to allow a supplier to reach large parts of the market through a handful of partners.

This study provides foreign manufacturers and brand owners with a practical reference for entering the Swiss market with branded or private-label (no-name) products across all categories presented at trade fairs such as Kind + Jugend in Cologne: nursery equipment, prams and strollers, car seats, furniture and textiles, feeding and care, safety products, baby and children's fashion, and toys for babies and toddlers.

Key findings:

• Market size: The core Swiss market for baby and toddler products (children aged 0–3, including nursery hardgoods, apparel, hygiene, food and infant/pre-school toys) is estimated at roughly CHF 1.2–1.5 billion at retail value. The total traditional toy market alone reached CHF 555 million in 2025 (+5.7% year-on-year), and grew a further 7.8% in value in the first half of 2026.

• Demography: Births have declined for four consecutive years but the decline almost stopped in 2025 (–0.1%). Lower birth numbers are offset by high spending per child, older and higher-income parents, and strong gifting by grandparents.

• Retail structure: Migros and Coop, together with Manor and other department stores, account for roughly half of the toy market. Specialist toy retail is consolidating (Franz Carl Weber is being absorbed into the Müller drugstore chain), while online retail – led by Galaxus, now the largest B2C online shop in Switzerland – is growing fastest.

• Importers and distributors play a decisive role. Most foreign brands are represented by an exclusive Swiss general agent (Generalvertretung) that handles logistics, trilingual marketing and retail key accounts. This study lists more than 40 relevant importers, distributors and directly importing retailers with website, general e-mail address and switchboard number wherever these are published.

• Market access: Switzerland is not an EU member, but its product-safety law is largely harmonised with EU rules. Since 1 January 2024 Switzerland has abolished import duties on industrial goods, so toys, textiles, prams and furniture enter duty-free from any origin; only VAT (8.1%) is due on import. Car seats must comply with UN R129 since 1 September 2024.

• Best opportunities: premium and design-led nursery products, sustainable/organic textiles and sleepwear, outdoor and mobility products adapted to Swiss lifestyles (bike trailers, balance bikes, weather-proof clothing), wooden and Montessori-type toys, games and puzzles, and eco-oriented hygiene and care products. For no-name suppliers, private-label programmes of the large grocers and discounters offer volume opportunities.
mercado-de-frutas-exoticas-alemanha:
A Alemanha é um dos maiores e mais ricos mercados consumidores de fruta fresca da Europa e, por não ter produção tropical própria, depende quase inteiramente de importação. Para produtores da África, da América Central e da América do Sul isso torna o mercado estruturalmente atraente — e, ao mesmo tempo, muito disputado e exigente. As oportunidades não estão no negócio de massa de banana e abacaxi, de margem baixa, mas no segmento premium e de especialidades — sobretudo abacate, frutas vermelhas, manga e maracujá — e nos nichos orgânico e Fairtrade.

A certificação é, na prática, o ingresso de entrada: do lado legal, o certificado fitossanitário e o cumprimento dos limites máximos de resíduos; do lado comercial, GLOBALG.A.P. e GRASP e, sobre eles, orgânico e/ou Fairtrade ou Rainforest Alliance. Para quem está começando, o caminho passa quase sempre por um importador estabelecido: fornecer diretamente às centrais de compra do varejo alemão — EDEKA Fruchtkontor, REWE Eurogroup — só se torna realista com volume, certificação completa e histórico comprovado. O fator decisivo é escolher importadores que de fato aceitam novos produtores, e a lista de contatos deste estudo é filtrada e classificada segundo esse critério.
fmcg-market-denmark:
Denmark is a small, wealthy market in which a few retail groups and buying organisations control the great majority of grocery volume. High purchasing power sits alongside some of the most demanding requirements in Europe on packaging, labelling and sustainability, and private label occupies a large and growing share of the shelf. For a foreign supplier that already sells abroad, the market rewards a partner who understands the Danish buyer's expectations rather than one who competes on price alone.

This study covers the fast-moving consumer goods sector across food and non-food, sets out market size and channel structure, profiles the leading retail groups, discounters and wholesale operators, explains the access requirements by supplier origin, and provides a directory of Danish FMCG importers and distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-kuwait:
Kuwait's foodservice market is estimated at roughly USD 3.5 billion in 2025 on a central estimate and is projected to reach approximately USD 5.3–5.6 billion by 2030–31. The demand profile is shaped by a population of about 4.4 million of which around 70% is expatriate, which produces unusually diverse cuisine demand for a market of this size, and by a concentration of spending in premium malls, corporate hubs and hotels.

For a foreign supplier this diversity is the opportunity: a product with a clear national or regional identity has a resident consumer base for it, which is not the case in every Gulf market. Retail and wholesale operators such as OnCost, Gulfmart and Carrefour sit alongside dedicated foodservice distributors, and the study profiles and classifies them by what they will actually take on from a new supplier. It covers market size and structure, the access requirements and documentation for foreign suppliers, the categories with the strongest prospects, and a directory of Kuwaiti importers and foodservice distributors.
fmcg-market-netherlands:
The Netherlands is a compact but affluent market of around 18 million consumers with high per-capita spending. Total retail reached around €138 billion in 2025, of which supermarkets accounted for around €51 billion; food and grocery together — food, beverages, household goods and tobacco — represent some 70 to 76 billion, of which roughly three-quarters is food. Non-food FMCG is substantial in its own right: mass beauty and personal care alone account for around €2.6 billion, premium beauty for €1.5 billion.

Buying power is strongly concentrated. Discounters Aldi and Lidl are the structural winners of recent years — Lidl at an estimated 10 to 11% market share, Aldi at around 6% and in 2025 the fastest grower. In addition, the buying cooperative Superunie bundles the volumes of some ten independent chains, including Plus, Coop and Dirk, which makes it a realistic point of contact for a newcomer. This study describes market size and channel structure for both food and non-food, the access requirements for suppliers from the EU and from outside, and contains an overview of Dutch FMCG importers, distributors and buying organisations.
baby-and-toddler-products-belgium:
Belgium is a small but affluent, highly urbanised market of about 11.9 million inhabitants, located at the logistic heart of Western Europe (port of Antwerp-Bruges, short distances to France, the Netherlands and Germany). With roughly 108,000 births per year, the market for baby and toddler products covering the Kind + Jugend scope (nursery hardgoods, furniture and textiles, feeding and care accessories, safety products, baby and toddler fashion and toys for 0–3 years) is estimated at EUR 550–700 million at retail value, rising to well above EUR 1 billion if nappies, baby food and formula are included.

Volume is under pressure: births fell to 108,033 in 2025, the lowest level since the war years, with the steepest decline in Wallonia and Brussels. Value is supported by premiumisation – parents buy fewer but better products, expect certified safety, sustainable materials and design – and by the strong Belgian birth-registry culture (geboortelijst / liste de naissance), which channels gift budgets from family and friends into specialist retailers.

The retail landscape has consolidated markedly since 2023. Colruyt divested both Dreamland (to ToyChamp) and Dreambaby (to the Vanhalst family's Supra Bazar), toy chain FUN went bankrupt and Orchestra-Prémaman shrank to nine Belgian stores. As a result, a small number of buying centres – Vanhalst Retail Group (Dreambaby, Supra Bazar, Kabine, Qiddo), DreamLand, Babydeals, the grocery groups, Action, HEMA and Kruidvat – control a large share of volume, while several hundred independent baby stores are supplied by a dense network of Belgian distributors, most of whom exhibit at Trademart Brussels.

For foreign suppliers the most promising routes are (1) an exclusive Benelux distribution agreement with a specialised distributor for branded products, (2) direct listing with the large specialist and discount chains for private label and good-value no-name ranges, and (3) marketplace sales via bol.com and Amazon.com.be to build awareness. EU suppliers enjoy free movement of goods; non-EU suppliers must appoint an EU-based economic operator, clear customs (usually in Antwerp) and ensure full compliance with EU product safety law before any listing.
baby-and-toddler-products-germany:
Germany is the largest market for baby and toddler products in Europe. According to Grand View Research, Germany accounted for roughly 22 % of European baby products revenue in 2025. The broadly defined market for baby and children’s outfitting (clothing, shoes, accessories, mobility, furniture and other first equipment) reached €7.12 billion in 2024 according to IFH Köln and BBE Handelsberatung, 3.8 % below the previous year; for 2025 a further decline of 1.9 % to just under €7 billion was forecast, followed by moderate growth of below 1 % p.a.

The market is shaped by two opposing forces: falling birth numbers (654,267 births in 2025, –3.4 %) and rising spending per child. IFH Köln puts spending on baby and children’s equipment in 2025 at around €2.36 billion (–2.2 %) but around €1,166 per child, almost 2 % more than in the previous year. Parents buy fewer items, but more consciously, and expect quality, safety and real benefit.

For foreign suppliers the most important entry routes are (1) specialised importers/distributors that build brands in the German-speaking (DACH) market, (2) buying groups for independent baby and toy retail (EK/happybaby, VEDES), (3) large specialist retailers that import directly (BabyOne, baby-walz/babymarkt, Smyths, online pure players) and (4) generalists – drugstores, discounters and textile discounters – that source private label and promotional goods. The regulatory framework is demanding (General Product Safety Regulation, product-specific EN standards, the new EU Toy Safety Regulation 2025/2509, chemicals and extended producer responsibility), but it is a strong barrier against low-quality competition and rewards well-prepared suppliers.
baby-and-toddler-products-ireland:
Ireland is a small but affluent, English-speaking market of about 5.4 million people with roughly 54,000 births per year (54,125 registered in 2025). Births have fallen by almost 18% in a decade and the average age of first-time mothers has risen to 31.8 years – which means fewer, older and financially stronger parents who spend more per child and favour safety, quality and premium design.

We estimate the Irish retail market for baby and toddler products (0–6 years, Kind+Jugend scope plus baby consumables and clothing) at roughly €0.60–0.75 billion at retail prices. Toys and nursery hardgoods account for about 40% of this, clothing for around a quarter, and nappies, baby food and baby care for the rest.

The market structure is unusual: distribution was historically run from the UK, and many brands are still sold into Ireland by “UK & Ireland” distributors. Since Brexit (and the loss of Mothercare Ireland in 2020) there is a clear need for EU-based supply chains and Irish-based distribution partners, and space for new brands in nursery specialist retail, online and discount non-food.

Key opportunities for foreign suppliers:

• Nursery hardgoods with a safety story – i-Size car seats (R129), lightweight travel systems, next-to-me cribs, smart monitors – sold via specialists such as Tony Kealys, All4Baby, Kaliedy and distributors like Baby Bedibies and Clever Clogs.

• Private label for Penneys, Dunnes Stores, Aldi, Lidl, Smyths and Kaliedy (babywear, textiles, feeding accessories, baby toys, value car seats and furniture).

• Toys: Smyths (one listing = up to seven countries), Toymaster independents and discount variety chains.

• Sustainable and premium products (organic textiles, wooden toys, Scandinavian design) for department stores and boutiques. Access is straightforward for EU suppliers (single market, CE marking, English labelling). Suppliers from the UK and other non-EU countries need customs formalities, an EU-based economic operator for product-safety purposes (GPSR) and must not rely on UKCA marking. The zero VAT rate on children’s clothing and footwear and the reduced 13.5% rate on child car seats are relevant for price positioning.
fmcg-market-austria:
Austria is a small but affluent market: around nine million inhabitants with high per-capita spending and a retail landscape in which a few chains and buying groups bundle the great majority of volume. For a foreign manufacturer that means fewer doors, but every listing decision carries correspondingly greater weight. The food retail sector is shaped by full-range retailers and discounters, while the cash & carry and delivered wholesale business opens access for foodservice, retail and resellers and is therefore often the more realistic point of entry.

This study looks at both halves of the sector, food and non-food, sets out market volume and channel structure, names the leading retail and wholesale players, explains the access requirements for suppliers from the EU, from non-EU Europe and from outside Europe, and contains a directory of Austrian FMCG importers and distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-china:
China's foodservice sector is worth on the order of USD 800–900 billion. The US Department of Agriculture put it at about USD 812 billion in 2025, up 3.2% year on year, while industry researchers place the commercial profit sector at roughly CNY 6.4 trillion — about USD 896 billion — for 2024 and forecast growth toward USD 0.9–1.1 trillion by the end of the decade. The wider food and beverage market, retail and foodservice combined, is worth some USD 1.3–1.7 trillion. China is also the world's second-largest importer of food and agricultural products, buying around USD 207 billion in 2025, with meat, fruit, aquatic products, grains and dairy each individually exceeding USD 10 billion.

One structural fact shapes every entry plan: China has no single dominant broadline distributor equivalent to Sysco in the United States. Coverage is assembled from regional distributors, category specialists and import agents, which means a foreign supplier is choosing a set of partners rather than one, and the sequence in which they are approached matters. This study covers market size and structure, the distribution landscape, the access requirements and documentation for foreign suppliers, the categories with the strongest prospects, and a directory of Chinese importers and foodservice distributors.
toy-market-germany:
Germany is the largest single toy market in continental Europe. Sales at end-consumer prices across all distribution channels came to around EUR 4.4 billion in 2024, and the German toy trade association (BVS), together with Circana, expected growth of about three percent for 2025. The market is attractive precisely because it is demanding: product safety rules are strict and are being tightened further, and retail buying is concentrated in comparatively few hands.

Between a good product and shelf space in Germany there is, as a rule, an importer or distributor, not the retailer itself. This study is aimed at manufacturers and brand owners outside Germany that already sell successfully in their home market and now want to enter under their own brand or as a private-label supplier. It covers traditional toys, games and puzzles, trading cards, video games as an adjacent category, and playground, nursery and school equipment. At its core is a directory of German importers, distributors, buying associations and direct-importing retailers, which deliberately distinguishes toy specialists from more broadly based non-food importers — the two negotiate differently and expect different things from a new supplier.
baby-and-toddler-products-united-kingdom:
The United Kingdom is one of Europe’s largest and most open markets for baby and toddler products, but it is also a mature, highly competitive and increasingly regulated market in which the number of births is falling. In 2025, 585,396 babies were born in England and Wales – 1.6% fewer than in 2024 and the lowest number since 1977; including Scotland and Northern Ireland, the UK records roughly 640,000–650,000 births a year. Demand in volume terms is therefore shrinking, while value is supported by premiumisation, innovation, gifting and higher average prices.

Measured across the full scope of Kind + Jugend categories (hardlines, nursery furniture and textiles, babywear, infant and preschool toys, feeding and care accessories), the retail value of the UK market can be estimated at approximately £3.0–3.8 billion per year, excluding baby food, formula and nappies. Adjacent markets are considerably larger: the total UK toy market reached £3.9 billion in 2025 (+6%), with infant and preschool toys delivering their strongest performance since 2017, and the entire UK childrenswear market is valued at around £7.85 billion. Specialist retailing of durable baby goods (prams, car seats, furniture) contracted to about £782 million in 2025 (−9.4%), reflecting the shift of sales to online players, department stores, grocers and general retailers.

Key conclusions for foreign suppliers:

• Brand route: Most foreign brands enter through an independent UK distributor that holds stock, services the many independent nursery retailers and negotiates with national accounts. Several distributors are currently reorganising portfolios (e.g. Hippychick restructuring, Inglesina leaving CuddleCo, Skip Hop moving to BTL Diffusion), which opens doors for new brands in 2026/27.

• Private-label route: Grocers (Tesco/F&F, Asda/George, Sainsbury’s/Tu), value fashion (Primark, Matalan), Next, M&S, Boots (expanding its own Boots Baby range while its Mothercare franchise ends), Mamas & Papas, JoJo Maman Bébé and discounters buy directly from manufacturers – typically requiring ethical audits, lab-tested compliance and competitive landed prices.

• Market access: CE marking remains accepted indefinitely in Great Britain for toys and most consumer products, so EU-compliant goods can in principle be sold without UKCA marking. However, several GB-specific rules apply –above all the Furniture and Furnishings (Fire) (Safety) Regulations 1988, the Nightwear (Safety) Regulations 1985, the PSTI cyber-security rules for connected products, and the requirement for a UK-based importer name and address.

• Tariffs: EU-origin goods enter duty-free under the EU–UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement (with proof of origin). Suppliers from Turkey, EFTA states, Japan, Korea, Vietnam and CPTPP partners benefit from free-trade agreements; since 15 July 2026 the UK–India agreement also reduces tariffs on Indian clothing and textiles. Chinese goods pay the UK Global Tariff (most toys 0%, prams around 2%, babywear up to 12%).

• Best opportunities: R129 car seats and lightweight travel systems, safe-sleep products, sensory/Montessori and wooden toys, infant carriers, innovative feeding and breastfeeding products, sustainable/organic textiles, convertible nursery furniture and gift-ready products.
exotic-fruits-market-germany:
Germany is one of the largest and most solvent markets for fresh fruit in Europe and, lacking its own tropical production, depends almost entirely on imports. For producers from Africa, Central and South America the market is therefore structurally attractive — yet at the same time fiercely competitive and demanding. The opportunities lie not in the low-margin mass business with bananas and pineapples, but in the premium and speciality segment, above all avocado, berries, mango and passion fruit, as well as in the organic and Fairtrade niches.

Certification is in practice the entry ticket: legally the phytosanitary certificate and compliance with maximum residue levels, on the trade side GLOBALG.A.P. and GRASP, and building on that organic and/or Fairtrade or Rainforest Alliance. For newcomers the route almost always leads through an established importer; direct supply to the retail purchasing organisations — EDEKA Fruchtkontor, REWE Eurogroup — only becomes realistic with volume, full certification and references. What matters is selecting importers that genuinely take on new growers; the contact list in this study has been filtered and assessed on that basis.
horeca-foodservice-market-germany:
The German out-of-home market is the second-largest sales channel for food in Germany after grocery retail: in 2025, consumers spent around €88.6 billion on food and beverages away from home, about 2% more than the previous year and around 7% above the 2019 level. Nominal growth, however, masks the sixth consecutive year of real, inflation-adjusted declines. Operators are under strong cost pressure, guests are unusually price-sensitive, and buyers are accordingly open to products that reduce food costs, save kitchen labour or enable a higher-margin position on the menu.

For foreign suppliers, one structural fact is decisive: German HoReCa operators almost never buy directly from the foreign manufacturer — 90 to 95% of volume flows through wholesalers and importers. Market entry is therefore decided by a listing with a wholesaler, not by selling to the kitchen. At the top are METRO, Transgourmet/Selgros, CHEFS CULINAR and EDEKA Foodservice; below them, buying groups such as Service-Bund, INTERGAST and TIFA bundle several hundred regional wholesalers and are often the more realistic entry point for newcomers. This study sets out market figures, channel structure and access requirements for EU and non-EU suppliers along this logic, and includes a directory of German importers and foodservice wholesalers.
horeca-foodservice-market-singapore:
Singapore is a high-income city-state of roughly 5.9 million residents plus a large tourist and expatriate population. Published estimates of its foodservice market range from about US$9.1 billion for 2025 on a narrow operator-revenue basis to around US$15.2 billion at the higher end, with broader value-chain estimates reaching US$22–29 billion; the commercial profit sector was estimated at about S$15.1 billion, roughly US$11.3 billion, in 2024 and is projected to grow towards some S$18.4 billion by 2029.

The defining feature of this market is that Singapore imports more than 90% of its food, sourced from over 180 countries and regions. There is effectively no domestic agricultural production to displace: the question is not whether to import but through which importer, and at what price and quality — which makes the market unusually accessible to a well-prepared supplier and intensely competitive at the same time. The channel is served by established distributors supplying hotels, chains and caterers, among them Bidfood Singapore, Culina, FoodXervices, Lim Siang Huat and Country Foods. This study sets out market size and structure under each definition, profiles those distributors, explains the access requirements and documentation for foreign suppliers, identifies the categories with the strongest prospects, and provides a directory of Singaporean importers and foodservice distribution partners.
horeca-foodservice-market-south-africa:
The South African foodservice market is estimated at about USD 10.2 billion in 2025 and is forecast to roughly double by 2030. Wider definitions that include all food and drink sold for out-of-home consumption put annual industry revenues considerably higher, in the region of USD 33 billion — a gap worth understanding before quoting a figure, because the two numbers describe different things rather than contradicting each other.

South Africa is the most developed foodservice supply chain on the continent, with established distributors, cash & carry operators and modern retail groups that buy for both retail and the professional channel, which makes it a realistic first African market for a supplier that has not exported to the region before. This study sets out market size and structure under each definition, profiles the distributors and importers that serve professional kitchens, explains the access requirements, documentation and import formalities for foreign suppliers, identifies the product groups with the strongest prospects, and provides a directory of South African importers and foodservice distribution partners.
horeca-foodservice-market-united-arab-em:
Published estimates of the UAE foodservice market for 2025 cluster between roughly USD 18.6 billion and USD 23.2 billion, with 2026 estimates around USD 27 billion and forecasts reaching USD 50–68 billion by 2033–2034 at double-digit compound growth. Mordor Intelligence, IMARC, Research & Markets, Renub Research and Market Data Forecast all publish figures in that band; the spread comes from scope rather than from any disagreement that this is one of the fastest-growing foodservice markets in the world.

Two structural features matter for a foreign supplier. The country imports the great majority of what its kitchens use, so imported supply is the norm rather than the exception. And there is no Metro or Makro-style pan-market cash-and-carry chain: the wholesale function sits with dedicated foodservice distributors, Bidfood Middle East (Horeca Trade LLC) being the largest in the country, alongside operators such as Admirals, Chef Middle East and Aramtec. This study covers market size and structure under each published definition, profiles those distributors, explains the access requirements and documentation for foreign suppliers, identifies the categories with the strongest prospects, and provides a directory of UAE importers and foodservice distributors.
fmcg-market-norway:
Fast-Moving Consumer Goods (FMCG) — also called Consumer Packaged Goods (CPG) — are everyday products that sell quickly, at relatively low unit prices, and are repurchased frequently. They are characterised by high volume, high turnover, thin margins per unit, wide distribution and short shelf-life or fast replacement cycles. In practice the FMCG universe is split into two broad blocks:

• Food FMCG: ambient/dry groceries, dairy, chilled and frozen foods, bakery, confectionery and snacks, coffee, tea and cocoa, soft drinks and water, beer, cider and (through the state monopoly) wine and spirits, baby food, fresh fruit and vegetables, and ‘world foods’.

• Non-food FMCG: personal care and cosmetics, household cleaning and laundry, paper and hygiene products, pet food and pet care, health & wellness/supplements, and seasonal / general-merchandise consumables sold alongside groceries. This study covers the whole FMCG spectrum — food and non-food alike. The common denominator for an international supplier is the importer / distributor: the Norwegian partner that buys, imports, warehouses and sells on to retail and foodservice. Because Norway’s grocery trade is unusually concentrated and its import rules for food are stricter than in the EU, the importer is the single most important gateway for a foreign brand or private-label product — they hold the shelf relationships, can register products correctly, and can move goods in the large volumes the market requires.
horeca-foodservice-market-malta:
Malta's food and drink service industry is estimated at roughly €1.2 billion in 2026 across some 2,600 businesses, having grown at double-digit annual rates since 2020, with a further €159 million or so in dedicated catering and foodservice contracting across about 440 businesses. The engine is tourism: around 3.56 million visitors arrived in 2024, up 19.5%, and total tourist expenditure of approximately €3.3 billion in 2024 is rising towards €3.9 billion in 2025.

For a foreign supplier the consequence is a market whose demand profile is set by visitors rather than residents — international menus, seasonal peaks and a hotel and restaurant base that expects imported range as a matter of course, since domestic production covers very little of it. Malta is an EU member, which places EU suppliers inside free circulation and gives suppliers from outside the Union a single defined set of requirements. This study covers market size and structure, the importers and distributors that serve the channel, the access requirements by supplier origin, and a directory of Maltese importers and foodservice distribution partners.
horeca-foodservice-market-switzerland:
The Swiss out-of-home market is today estimated at around CHF 30 billion a year; GastroSuisse already reported about CHF 23.6 billion in 2017, and the figure has grown since. Independent analyses put the commercial foodservice market for 2024 at roughly USD 16 to 17 billion, with expected annual growth of around 5 to 8 percent. Purchasing power and price levels make Switzerland attractive to foreign suppliers — and demanding at the same time.

The route to the customer runs through a handful of strong wholesalers. Transgourmet/Prodega (Coop) is the clear market leader; Saviva (Migros), Aligro/CCA Angehrn, TopCC (Spar) and the Pistor cooperative make up the rest of the leading group. Coop and Migros together control around a quarter of foodservice supply. For a new supplier, market entry therefore hinges on being listed with one of these houses. The study sets out market volume and channel structure, explains the access requirements for suppliers from the EU and from third countries, and includes a directory of Swiss importers and foodservice wholesalers.
fmcg-market-sweden:
Sweden is a high-income market where a small number of organised retail groups dominate grocery, supported by buying alliances and a strong private-label culture. Two features shape the route to market: retail alcohol is sold only through the state monopoly, so beverage suppliers must work through importers and the on-trade separately; and the buyer's expectations on sustainability, packaging and product documentation are among the strictest in Europe.

This study covers the food and non-food fast-moving consumer goods sector, sets out market size and channel structure, profiles the leading retail groups and wholesalers, explains the access requirements for suppliers from the EU, from non-EU Europe and from outside Europe, and provides a directory of Swedish FMCG importers and distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-belgium:
Out-of-home food spending in Belgium is put at around EUR 15 billion in 2023, with a projection of about EUR 17 billion by 2028; the broader hotel and restaurant turnover would rise from about EUR 20 billion to 24 billion over the same period. Placed in the Benelux context, the whole represents USD 40 billion to 43 billion in 2025-2026, with annual growth of close to 5.7% expected to 2031.

The structural constraint of the Belgian market is labour cost: about EUR 48 an hour according to Eurostat, which squeezes operators' margins and makes buyers particularly receptive to products that cut kitchen preparation time or ingredient cost. On the distribution side, Sligro Food Group Belgium — with Sligro-ISPC and JAVA Foodservice — holds a leading position following its acquisitions. This study presents the market's volume and structure, the main operators, the access conditions according to the supplier's origin and the categories with the strongest potential, and includes a directory of Belgian importers and distributors in out-of-home catering.
fruit-bars-and-cereal-bars-france:
Published estimates put the French cereal bar market at around €162 million on a narrow definition (retail cereal bars, 2024), with growth of around 3% a year that would take it to some €226 million by 2035. Broadening the scope to all bars — cereal, fruit, protein and snacks — a realistic working estimate lies between €450 and €600 million. At European level, the cereal bar market is valued at around $4.4 billion in 2026.

Access plays out against a highly concentrated distribution: six groups control the food market — E.Leclerc (around 24%), Carrefour (21%), Intermarché (17.5%), Coopérative U (13%), Auchan (8.5%) and Lidl (8%) — and buying alliances concentrate that power even further, with Concordis (Carrefour and Coopérative U) representing more than 34% of buying power and Aura Retail (Intermarché, Auchan, Casino) more than 29%. Organic represents a distinct entry route: the market returned to growth in 2025 at €12.6 billion (+3.6%), with specialised stores growing 8.5%. This study includes a directory of French importers and distributors in the sector.
horeca-foodservice-market-ecuador:
Ecuador is a dollarised economy of some 18.3 million inhabitants, with a median age close to 29 and roughly two-thirds urban population. Dollarisation removes currency risk for the foreign supplier, an unusual factor in the region. Total agricultural imports run at around USD 4.3 billion a year, of which about USD 1 billion is consumer-oriented food; the main suppliers are Chile (~21%), Colombia (~17%), Peru (~10%) and the United States.

Retail trade is estimated at around USD 27 billion, with a growing share for modern supermarkets, and tourism is the main growth driver of the channel, with around 1.4 million international arrivals. This study sets out the market's volume and structure, the distribution channels and their operators, the access and certification requirements according to the supplier's origin and the categories with the best prospects, and includes a directory of Ecuadorian importers and distributors in the HORECA channel.
horeca-foodservice-market-argentina:
Estimates of the Argentine restaurant market range between USD 17 billion and USD 35 billion for 2025 depending on the scope and the source: IMARC puts it at around USD 17.6 billion, with a projection of some USD 45.7 billion for 2034 at a compound rate of close to 11% a year, while Bonafide estimates it at about USD 35 billion. The commercial sector measured in local currency was around ARS 4.1 trillion in 2023, equivalent to some USD 14 billion, with very high nominal growth rates driven by inflation.

That dispersion means any figure must be read together with its definition, and this study identifies the source of every data point it cites. In distribution, cash & carry wholesale chains — Makro, Maxiconsumo, Diarco and Vital, among others — are the most realistic point of entry for a foreign supplier, ahead of direct sales to restaurants. The study sets out the market's volume and structure, the leading operators, the access requirements according to the supplier's origin and the categories with the strongest prospects, and includes a directory of Argentine importers and distributors in the HORECA channel.
horeca-foodservice-market-malaysia:
Recent market studies converge on a Malaysian foodservice value of about USD 14.75 billion for 2025, forecast to grow at roughly 13% a year to approximately USD 27.5 billion by 2030 and around USD 30.7 billion by 2031. That is one of the steepest growth curves in ASEAN, and it is being met substantially by imported supply rather than by domestic production alone.

For a foreign supplier, Malaysia's combination of a multi-ethnic domestic market, a well-developed modern retail and wholesale infrastructure and an established halal certification system makes it both accessible and a credible base from which to approach the wider region. This study sets out market size and structure, profiles the importers, distributors and cash & carry operators that serve hotels, restaurants and institutional kitchens, explains the access requirements and documentation for foreign suppliers including halal certification, identifies the product groups with the strongest prospects, and provides a directory of Malaysian importers and foodservice distribution partners.
fmcg-market-brazil:
Brazil is the largest consumer goods market in Latin America and one of the most complex to access. Distribution is concentrated in large chains and cash-and-carry formats, with regional groups growing in strength, while importing involves high taxation, its own regulatory requirements and a chain of importers and distributors specialised by category. For a foreign supplier, choosing the right partner often determines whether the product reaches the point of sale or gets stuck at the entry barrier.

This study defines the scope of consumer goods, structures the food and non-food market, identifies the leading retail and wholesale players, details the access requirements according to the supplier's origin, and brings together a directory of Brazilian importers and distributors.
fmcg-market-south-korea:
South Korea is one of Asia's most sophisticated and open consumer markets. It combines high household purchasing power, extreme urban density, a world-leading e-commerce and logistics infrastructure, and consumers who are exceptionally quick to adopt new products, brands and trends. For a foreign brand owner or supplier, this makes South Korea a demanding but rewarding target: shelf life for weak concepts is short, but genuinely differentiated products can scale nationally very fast.

This study is written as a stand-alone reference for exporters who already sell successfully in their home market and want to introduce their brand — or supply private label — into South Korea. It explains what FMCG means, sizes the market, maps the players and channels, sets out the concrete access requirements (distinguishing suppliers from the EU, from non-EU Europe, and from outside Europe), highlights the product categories with the best chances, and provides a categorised directory of relevant importers and distributors with verified public contact details.

Key take-aways: (1) The market rewards “better-for-you”, premium, convenient and clean-label products; the consumer shift is clearly from indulgence towards function. (2) Almost every foreign supplier needs a Korea-registered importer of record — the importer, not the exporter, carries the regulatory responsibility. (3) South Korea is one of the most FTA-connected economies in the world, so EU (and most European) suppliers enjoy near-zero tariffs if origin is documented correctly, while suppliers from countries without a free-trade agreement pay the standard applied duty. (4) Regulatory obligations under the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety (MFDS) — facility registration, import declaration, inspection and Korean labelling — apply to all suppliers equally, regardless of tariff treatment.
fmcg-market-switzerland:
Switzerland is a small, very affluent market outside the EU, where two large cooperatives and the discounter shape food retail. The flip side of its attractiveness is its own barriers: customs and import regulations, different approval and labelling rules and strong price sensitivity in cross-border trade. For a foreign manufacturer an experienced importer or distributor is therefore usually the realistic route onto the shelf.

This study looks at food and non-food, sets out market volume and channel structure, names the leading retailers and wholesalers, explains the access requirements for suppliers from the EU and from third countries, and contains a directory of Swiss FMCG importers and distributors.
fmcg-market-united-arab-emirates:
This study is written for foreign manufacturers and suppliers — of both branded and private-label products —who want to sell fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). It covers what FMCG means, how large the market is, who the main players are, where the opportunities lie for newcomers, and what it takes to get products onto UAE shelves. It closes with a classified directory of relevant UAE importers and distributors, including verified head-office phone numbers, general contact addresses, and — where applicable —the route for proposing new products.

The central idea is simple: FMCG importers and distributors are the most efficient entry point for a foreign supplier. They hold the trade licences, product-registration accounts and customs codes required by law; they already have the shelf relationships with retailers and the hospitality trade; and they can move new brands and products in volume. The directory therefore focuses on companies that are both willing and able to introduce products that already sell well abroad — whether under the supplier's own brand or as a private label.
horeca-foodservice-market-tunisia:
Tunisia is a Mediterranean market of roughly 12 million residents whose foodservice demand is amplified by a large and recovering tourism sector. In 2024 the country recorded about 10.25 million tourist arrivals — its highest level since 2010 — generating tourism revenue of roughly TND 7.05 billion, about US$2.3 billion, equivalent to close to 9% of GDP and supporting on the order of 400,000 jobs. In 2025 arrivals surpassed 11 million.

The composition of that visitor base shapes the menu and therefore the supply opportunity: the leading source markets are Algeria with about 3.1 million arrivals, largely across the land border, followed by Libya (about 1.4 million), France (1.2 million), Germany (560,000), the United Kingdom (410,000) and Italy (380,000). A supplier from any of those origins is selling into a market where its products already have a resident audience for part of the year. This study sets out market size and structure, profiles the importers, distributors and retail groups that serve the channel, explains the access requirements and documentation for foreign suppliers, and provides a directory of Tunisian importers and foodservice distribution partners.
horeca-foodservice-market-paraguay:
Paraguay has a population of approximately 6.9 million with a notably young age profile: about half are in the lower reaches of the pyramid. In beverages, the domestic wine market is estimated at around 27 million litres a year, about USD 63 million, and beer at some 227 million litres, in the order of USD 480 million — two figures that give a concrete measure of the channel's consumption.

The Latin American restaurant market as a whole was estimated at about USD 170 billion in 2023, growing at a low single-digit compound rate; Paraguay is a small position within that total, with the advantage of limited foreign competition. This study covers the structure of the market and its channels, the main operators, the access and import requirements by supplier origin and the categories with the best prospects, and includes a directory of Paraguayan importers and distributors in the HORECA channel.
horeca-foodservice-market-south-korea:
South Korea offers roughly 51 million affluent, urban and digitally engaged consumers, concentrated heavily in the Seoul Capital Area. Estimates place the foodservice market at USD 120–140 billion in 2025, roughly KRW 150–190 trillion; several widely cited market-research houses put 2025 at about USD 126–138 billion and project continued strong growth, while USDA and ATO figures size the Hotel-Restaurant-Institutional sector at about KRW 140 trillion, around USD 122 billion.

The concentration of demand in one metropolitan region changes the entry calculation: national coverage is less important than the right partner in the capital area, and trends move quickly enough that a product's timing matters as much as its specification. This study sets out market size and structure, profiles the distributors, cash & carry operators and specialist importers that serve the channel, explains the access requirements for suppliers from the EU, from non-EU Europe and from outside Europe, identifies the product groups with the strongest prospects, and provides a directory of Korean importers and foodservice distributors.
toy-market-belgium:
Belgium is a small, wealthy and densely populated market of around 11.8 million inhabitants, located between three of Europe's largest markets. Its commercial particularity is first and foremost linguistic: the country has three official languages — Dutch, spoken by around 60% of the population in Flanders, French, around 40% in Wallonia and predominantly in Brussels, and German for a small community in the east. For a toy supplier, this shapes labelling, packaging and documentation from the very first order.

It is also a logistics hub heavily dependent on imports, with China alone supplying nearly half the imported value. A gap has opened recently: the average retail price has reached a record level while the average import price has fallen appreciably. The directory in chapter 8 lists Belgian importers, distributors, importing retailers and non-food wholesalers, distinguishing toy specialists from importers for whom toys are just one non-food category among many, and separating full-range importers, range specialists, institutional suppliers and large chains that import on their own account.
fmcg-market-france:
France is the second-largest consumer goods market in the European Union and one of the most concentrated retail landscapes in the world. For a foreign manufacturer whose brand already works in its home market, it is therefore a market that is both highly attractive and comparatively difficult to enter: five buying organisations control the great majority of food distribution, listing decisions are taken during an annual negotiation window governed by law, and national labelling and environmental rules go well beyond the European minimum.

On the wholesale and cash & carry side, access runs in particular through Metro France, Promocash (Carrefour group), Transgourmet France, Groupe Pomona, Sysco France and Francap Distribution. This study is addressed to suppliers who want to sell in France, not to market observers: it defines the scope of fast-moving consumer goods, measures and structures the market, identifies the players and European buying alliances, sets out the four realistic access routes — including private label as a volume route —, details the requirements applicable depending on whether the supplier is established in the EU, in non-EU Europe or outside Europe, and includes a directory of French importers and distributors.
