1. Executive summary

Luxembourg is the smallest and, at the same time, the most affluent FMCG market in the European Union. With about 691,000 residents on 1 January 2026, it is a small market in absolute terms, but it combines the highest price level for food in the EU, very high purchasing power, an extremely international population (46.6% foreign nationals, 180 nationalities) and roughly 232,000 cross-border commuters from France, Belgium and Germany who do part of their daily shopping in the Grand Duchy. Low excise duties on tobacco, alcohol and fuel additionally attract shoppers from the neighbouring regions. The retail landscape is concentrated. The Luxembourg family company Cactus is the historical market leader, followed by Delhaize (Ahold Delhaize), E.Leclerc (which took over the 27 former Cora, Match and Smatch stores at the end of 2023), Auchan, the discounters Lidl and Aldi, Colruyt and a number of independents such as Pall Center and the organic chain Naturata. Several of these chains buy centrally outside Luxembourg (Delhaize via Belgium, Leclerc via its regional buying centre in eastern France), which is a key point for foreign suppliers: in many categories the listing decision for Luxembourg is made in Brussels or in the French Grand Est region. The domestic importer and wholesale base is small but highly relevant. La Provençale (broadline wholesale and cash & carry with more than 40,000 references, serving HoReCa and retail across the Greater Region), Trendy Foods Luxembourg (proximity and convenience wholesale including non-food), the beverage group Munhowen (which has absorbed the non-HoReCa business of Boissons Heintz), the fresh-produce specialist Grosbusch, the organic wholesaler Biogros and a number of specialists for Portuguese, Italian and other products form the core of the import channel. Non-food FMCG (personal care, household, OTC health, pet) is mostly supplied directly to the retailers' central buying or via Belgian BeLux distributors; pharmacy-channel products run through the pharmaceutical wholesalers. Key takeaways for foreign suppliers • Think Greater Region and BeLux: Luxembourg is rarely approached in isolation. Many importers also sell into Lorraine, Wallonia and the Saarland/Trier region, and many brands serve Luxembourg through a Belgian distributor. • Premium, organic, convenience, plant-based and 'world food' (especially Portuguese, Italian, French, Balkan, Asian and Latin American) products fit the affluent, multicultural consumer base. • Packaging must carry mandatory information in French or German; Belgian FR/NL/DE packs and French or German packs are generally accepted in practice. • EU suppliers face no customs formalities; suppliers from non-EU Europe and overseas need an EU importer of record, customs clearance and, for products of animal origin and many plant products, official border controls. • Volumes per SKU are small; price the extra cost of small drops, multilingual labelling and listing fees into the business plan, or enter via a distributor who consolidates.
fmcg-market-new-zealand:
This study examines the New Zealand market for Fast-Moving Consumer Goods (FMCG) from the perspective of foreign manufacturers and suppliers who already sell successfully abroad and are considering entry into New Zealand – whether under their own brand or as a private-label supplier.

New Zealand is a mature, affluent, English-speaking consumer market of roughly 5.3 million people with high per-capita grocery spend. Its defining structural feature is one of the most concentrated grocery-retail landscapes in the developed world: two retail groups – Foodstuffs and Woolworths New Zealand – together control about 82% of grocery sales. For a foreign supplier, this has one dominant practical consequence: you almost never sell to the market directly. You sell through an importer, distributor or sales-and-marketing agency that already holds the retailer relationships, warehousing, compliance capability and buyer access needed to place a product on shelf.

Market access is decided far more by regulatory compliance and commercial fit than by country of origin. Since 1 May 2024 the EU–New Zealand Free Trade Agreement has removed New Zealand tariffs on all goods originating in the EU, so EU-based suppliers now enjoy duty-free access on the same terms that UK suppliers obtained under the UK–NZ FTA and that many other partners obtain under the CPTPP. The genuine hurdles are the same for everyone: registration as (or supply through) a registered food importer with the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI), full compliance with the Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code, and English-language labelling with a New Zealand supplier name and address.

The core of this document is a classified directory of relevant FMCG importers and distributors – the businesses most able and most likely to introduce a proven foreign brand or product to New Zealand. Each entry distinguishes food from non-food focus, channel type (retail, HoReCa/foodservice, cash & carry, full-range vs. specialist), the product categories carried, and whether the company positions itself primarily as a “brand-maker” (actively seeking new innovative brands) or as a distributor of established, well-known lines. Where a supplier portal or a page identifying buyers exists, it is linked; where a switchboard or general email is published, it is given.

Only companies with verifiable direct contact details are listed

This directory deliberately includes only companies that publish their own website and direct contact details (switchboard telephone and/or a general email address). Businesses without verifiable direct contact channels have been left out entirely, because leads that cannot be contacted directly are of no practical use to a supplier.
fmcg-market-people-s-republic-of-china:
This study is a practical reference for foreign manufacturers and suppliers that already sell successfully in their home market and want to enter the Chinese market for fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG). It covers the full FMCG spectrum – both food and non-food – and is written to help an exporter understand how large the market is, who the main players are, which product categories offer the best chances, what the regulatory requirements are, and, above all, which Chinese importers and distributors are able to introduce foreign brands (or private-label products) to the retail and foodservice trade in large volumes.

The heart of the study is a directory of relevant FMCG importers and distributors. FMCG importers are especially valuable partners for foreign suppliers because they hold the best connections into modern retail and the HoReCa / foodservice trade and can list new brands and products across many outlets at once. For every company we give a website and at least one direct contact channel; we distinguish importer types, product categories and the likely fit for new suppliers; and we indicate whether the company publishes a supplier or brand-proposal contact. In line with data-protection good practice, we do not list the personal names or personal e-mail addresses of individual buyers or managers, even where a company names them; instead we point to the official supplier channel.
fmcg-market-poland:
Poland is one of the largest and fastest-developing consumer markets in the EU, led by discount chains and a rapidly modernising convenience sector, with wholesale operators supplying independent retail and smaller regional chains. For a foreign supplier the market rewards speed and scale: several of the leading players are subsidiaries of large European groups, so European standards and documentation are already familiar on the buying side, but competition on shelf and price is intense.

This study measures and structures the fast-moving consumer goods market across food and non-food, profiles the leading grocery retailers, discounters and wholesalers, sets out the access requirements by supplier origin, and provides a directory of Polish FMCG importers and distributors.
fmcg-market-principality-of-liechtenstei:
Fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG), also called consumer packaged goods (CPG), are products that are bought frequently, sold in high volumes, consumed or used up quickly and sold at relatively low unit prices. Margins per unit are usually thin, so commercial success depends on volume, shelf availability, efficient logistics and strong trade relationships. Typical characteristics are:

• High purchase frequency (daily to monthly) and short shelf or usage life.

• Distribution through supermarkets, discounters, convenience stores, drugstores, pharmacies, cash-and-carry markets, foodservice wholesalers and e-commerce.

• Strong role of brands and private labels (retailer own brands) competing side by side on the shelf.

• Heavy reliance on promotions, listing agreements and category management with retailers. Main FMCG categories covered in this study:

FMCG importers and distributors are particularly attractive partners for foreign manufacturers because they already hold listings with retail and HoReCa customers, run the logistics and customs processes, and can introduce new brands and products in commercial volumes.
horeca-foodservice-market-algeria:
Algeria combines a population of roughly 45 to 46 million, a young demographic profile, advancing urbanisation and a strong dependence on imported food. For a foreign supplier that dependence is the entry point: a substantial share of what professional kitchens use is not produced domestically, so the competition is between importers and origins rather than against local production.

Modern retail chains are the visible face of organised distribution and several of them buy for both retail and foodservice — UNO (Numidis/Cevital), Ardis (Arcofina), Family Shop and Carrefour list branded products and are a realistic first approach for a supplier with a recognisable range. Alongside them sit dedicated importers and wholesalers serving hotels, restaurants and institutional kitchens. This study sets out the size and structure of the market, profiles those channels, explains the access requirements, documentation and import formalities that apply to foreign suppliers, identifies the product groups with the strongest prospects, and provides a directory of Algerian importers and distribution partners.
horeca-foodservice-market-australia:
The Australian foodservice market is put at roughly AUD 73 billion in 2025 and is forecast to grow at around 5.9% a year, approaching AUD 129 billion by the mid-2030s; other analyst houses place 2025 between about USD 67 billion and USD 90 billion depending on segment definitions, but all point to strong single-digit growth. GlobalData valued the profit sector at about AUD 86.6 billion in 2022. Full-service restaurants are the second-largest channel at roughly AUD 22.2 billion, and the coffee and tea shop segment — about AUD 3.7 billion and growing near 4.9% a year — sits on top of a national coffee market of some AUD 22 billion expanding at around 7.5% annually.

Distribution is dominated by a small number of national broadline distributors, Bidfood and PFD Food Services foremost among them, which means a foreign supplier's coverage decision is concentrated in a few conversations. Australia also applies strict biosecurity and import requirements that shape which products are realistic to bring in and in what form. This study covers market size and structure, the leading players, the access requirements by supplier origin, the categories with the strongest prospects, and a directory of Australian importers and foodservice distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-austria:
Austria is a small market by population — around 9.2 million people — but an unusually large one in gastronomy, because the country feeds far more people than it accommodates. In 2025 Austria recorded 157.27 million overnight stays and 48.17 million arrivals, both record highs. Some 55,000 foodservice businesses generate around EUR 14.5 billion in turnover and employ more than 153,000 people; together with accommodation, the hospitality sector reaches about EUR 23.3 billion.

Access runs through a manageable number of wholesalers: Transgourmet, METRO, Wedl, Eurogast, Kröswang and Kastner account for the bulk of national volume and together report more than EUR 3.8 billion in turnover. The channel has shifted markedly from cash-and-carry to delivered wholesale — among the leading groups, around 70 to 78 percent of business is now delivery. This study describes market volume and channel structure, the access requirements for suppliers from the EU and from third countries, and the product groups with the best prospects, and includes a directory of Austrian importers and gastronomy wholesalers.
horeca-foodservice-market-bolivia:
Bolivia is a small but underserved Andean market, with some 12 million inhabitants, a young and urbanising consumer base, and consumption concentrated in a few urban centres. Within a Latin American restaurant market estimated at between USD 170 billion and 200 billion, Bolivia represents a small fraction — and that is precisely why competition among foreign suppliers is far weaker than in the region's large markets.

For a supplier, the practical consequence is that national coverage is achieved with a very small number of partners, and that the first well-chosen distributor weighs more than in any mature market. This study sets out the structure of the market and its channels, the main distribution operators, the access and import requirements according to the supplier's origin and the product categories with the best prospects, and includes a directory of Bolivian importers and distributors in the HORECA channel.
horeca-foodservice-market-brazil:
Sales by the food industry to Brazilian food service were projected by ABIA at BRL 287.1 billion for 2025, a nominal rise of about 10% over the BRL 260.9 billion of 2024 and approximately 28.3% of the country's entire food industry output. The Instituto Foodservice Brasil counts around 1.6 million active establishments. By comparison, food retail turned over BRL 1.145 trillion in 2025, equivalent to about 9% of GDP, of which BRL 327.7 billion — 29% — in cash & carry alone.

International estimates vary widely according to the definition adopted: houses such as Mordor Intelligence and Market Data Forecast place Brazilian food service between USD 18 billion and 19 billion in 2025, with compound growth close to 7% a year, while the IMARC Group reaches USD 55.6 billion using a broader perimeter of establishments. This study brings together the size and structure of the market, the main distribution and cash & carry operators, the access requirements according to the supplier's origin and the categories with the best prospects, plus a directory of Brazilian importers and distributors in the food service channel.
horeca-foodservice-market-bulgaria:
Bulgaria is a compact but dynamic South-East European market of roughly 6.4 million people and a full member of the European Union, which places EU suppliers inside free circulation and gives non-EU suppliers a single, well-defined set of entry rules. Total food and agricultural imports ran to approximately USD 7.57 billion in 2023, about 12% below the 2022 peak. Some categories are setting records rather than retreating: fish and seafood imports reached about USD 175.1 million in 2024, up 3% on 2023, with the foodservice sector a significant part of that demand.

Professional supply is led by cash & carry. METRO Bulgaria is the dominant self-service wholesaler for professional customers and alone reports annual turnover in the order of half a billion euro, which makes it the single most consequential listing decision for most new suppliers. Around it sit delivered foodservice distributors and category specialists. This study sets out market size and structure, profiles the operators that matter, explains the access requirements for suppliers from the EU, from non-EU Europe and from outside Europe, and provides a directory of Bulgarian importers and foodservice distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-canada:
Commercial foodservice sales in Canada are estimated in the region of CAD 115–135 billion for 2025 across the major analyst houses — GlobalData puts the profit sector at about CAD 128.7 billion — and the sector employs roughly 1.2 million people. Full-service restaurants account for around USD 49.5 billion across some 79,000 locations and quick service for about USD 37 billion across some 21,000. Post-pandemic eating-out habits, immigration-driven demand for global flavours and a strong premiumisation trend all favour suppliers with a distinctive product of origin.

The route to the plate is unusually well defined. Distribution has consolidated to two national broadline distributors — Sysco Canada and Gordon Food Service — which carry a full range and deliver coast to coast, and which are therefore the realistic first partners for a foreign brand. Cash-and-carry channels including Costco Business Centre, Wholesale Club and GFS Stores serve independent operators who self-serve. This study covers market size and structure, the leading players, the access requirements for suppliers from the EU, from non-EU Europe and from outside Europe, the product groups with the strongest prospects, and a directory of Canadian importers and foodservice distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-colombia:
Colombia is Latin America's third most populous country, with some 52 million inhabitants and close to 80% urban population. The total restaurant market is valued at around USD 13 billion to 14 billion for 2025, driven by urbanisation, rising disposable income and the habit of eating out, with forecasts of double-digit compound growth in the coming years.

For a foreign supplier, urban concentration is an operational advantage: it makes it possible to cover a very high share of demand through a small number of distributors and locations. This study sets out the market's volume and structure, the distribution channels and their main operators, the access and certification requirements according to the supplier's origin and the product categories with the best prospects, and includes a directory of Colombian importers and distributors in the HORECA channel.
horeca-foodservice-market-croatia:
Croatia has a resident population of roughly 3.8 million but welcomed more than 20 million tourists and over 100 million overnight stays — a ratio that makes its foodservice market far larger than its population suggests, and intensely seasonal. The sector is valued at approximately €2.7 billion in 2026, of which restaurants and takeaways account for about €2.4 billion across roughly 7,700 businesses, the single largest channel. The accommodation market adds a further US$5.7–6.1 billion and is growing at about 6.5% a year to 2031.

Professional supply runs through cash & carry, led nationally by METRO, and through distributors that are typically either part of large domestic groups — Fortenova, Atlantic, Orbico — or subsidiaries of international wholesalers. Knowing which of the two a potential partner belongs to matters, because it determines the decision process and what will be expected of a new supplier. Own-brand ranges such as METRO Chef and METRO Professional are an explicit private-label route in. This study covers market size and structure, the distribution channels, access requirements by supplier origin, and a directory of Croatian importers and foodservice distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-czech-republic:
The Czech consumer foodservice market — restaurants, hotels, quick service and institutional catering — is estimated in the order of USD 11–13 billion a year, having returned to growth after the pandemic. It is a market in which a single well-chosen partner can carry a product a long way, because the top of the distribution channel is unusually concentrated.

Bidfood Czech Republic is the reference distributor. Part of Bidcorp, the world's second-largest foodservice group after Sysco, it carries around 5,000 SKUs, operates its own delivery network and runs Bidfood Expo, the largest professional gastronomy event in Czechia and Slovakia — which makes it a strategic contact well beyond its order book. Alongside it, MAKRO (Metro Group) covers the cash & carry side. This study sets out market size and structure, profiles the broadline distributors, cash & carry operators and category specialists, explains the access requirements for suppliers from the EU, from non-EU Europe and from outside Europe, and provides a directory of Czech importers and foodservice distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-denmark:
The Danish out-of-home profit sector — restaurants, hotels, cafés, bars, catering and travel — generated revenue of approximately DKK 85 billion (around USD 12.3 billion) in 2023, up from about DKK 78 billion before the pandemic in 2019. Full-service restaurants are the largest single channel at roughly 36% of profit-sector value, followed by quick-service and the pub and bar segment.

Distribution is highly concentrated: three broadline groups — Dansk Cater, Dagrofa Foodservice and Hørkram — dominate, and most operators are reached mainly through them. For a foreign supplier that cuts both ways: the number of doors to knock on is small, but each listing decision carries disproportionate weight. This study assesses the market from the perspective of a supplier that already sells successfully abroad and now wants to introduce its brands or supply private-label products in Denmark. It sets out the access requirements for suppliers from the EU, from non-EU Europe and from outside Europe, and provides a directory of Danish importers and foodservice distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-egypt:
Egypt is the most populous country in the Arab world, with around 118 million inhabitants, a gross domestic product of approximately USD 389 billion and a very young population. Its foodservice market is correspondingly large, and demand is growing from a demographic base rather than from a cyclical recovery — which is a different kind of opportunity from the mature European markets, and calls for a different pricing and packaging strategy.

For a foreign supplier the questions that decide an entry are less about market size than about mechanics: which importers hold the registrations, how currency and payment terms are handled, and which product formats survive the local cold chain and price expectations. This study sets out the size and structure of the market, profiles the importers, distributors and cash & carry operators that serve professional kitchens, explains the access requirements and documentation for foreign suppliers including halal certification, identifies the product groups with the strongest prospects, and provides a directory of Egyptian importers and foodservice distribution partners.
horeca-foodservice-market-estonia:
Estonia is a small but affluent, highly digital EU and eurozone market of roughly 1.37 million people, with high GDP per capita for the region. Total food expenditure was about €3.4 billion in 2023 and is projected to reach around €4.2 billion by 2028, an average growth of some 3.6% a year; food retail sales are forecast to rise from about €2.0 billion to €2.3 billion over the same period, while grocery retail alone is estimated at around €3.9 billion in 2025.

One feature makes Estonia more attractive than its size suggests: although this study targets foodservice, the same importers frequently also supply the grocery chains, so a single relationship can open two channels, and their private-label programmes are an adjacent opportunity for a supplier without brand recognition. The leading grocery players are Selver (Tallinna Kaubamaja Grupp), Maxima, Rimi (Salling Group), Prisma (S Group), Grossi Toidukaubad and the discounter Lidl. This study covers market size and structure, the distribution landscape, access requirements by supplier origin, and a directory of Estonian importers and foodservice distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-finland:
Finland is a market of about 5.6 million people with an established eating-out culture. Foodservice at end-consumer level generates in the region of €5.6 billion in sales across roughly 10,000 businesses, while the professional wholesale layer that supplies it is worth roughly €2.3 billion (2023) and is forecast to reach about €2.8 billion by 2028, a compound rate of around 4.1% a year. Some 16,150 professional kitchens serve close to 749 million meals annually.

Two sub-segments deserve a foreign supplier's attention because they are both sizeable and growing: wholesale to ethnic restaurants — sushi, Chinese, Indian, Nepalese, Thai and Vietnamese — was worth around €383 million in 2023, and wholesale to pizzerias, burger and kebab restaurants around €196 million. Both are served largely by specialist importers rather than by the broadline majors, which lowers the entry threshold for a supplier with a distinctive product of origin. This study covers market size and structure, the leading players, the access requirements by supplier origin, and a directory of Finnish importers and foodservice distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-france:
Out-of-home food consumption reached about €128.3 billion in France in 2025, up 4.2% year on year, for close to 12 billion meals served. Growth is now almost entirely driven by value: the number of meals served has remained virtually flat. Full-service commercial restaurants account for about €46.9 billion (+3.2%), fast food and counter service about €28.6 billion (+3.7%), and alternative channels — in-store takeaway, bakeries and similar — about €25.4 billion.

Between manufacturers and kitchens sits a distribution layer worth about €24.7 billion, which is steadily consolidating: the top five operators — METRO, Groupe Pomona, France Frais, Transgourmet and Distriboissons — now hold close to 58%. For a foreign supplier, that is where market entry is decided: a listing is won with a wholesaler or importer, not with the chef. This study presents the market's volume and structure, the main players, the access requirements by supplier origin (EU, non-EU Europe, outside Europe), the most promising product categories, and a directory of French importers and foodservice distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-greece:
Greek foodservice turnover is in the region of US$13–14 billion; GlobalData valued the market at about US$13.6 billion for 2021. For a foreign supplier the practical consequence of the country's structure is that seasonality and the tourist trade shape both the volume curve and the product mix, so a listing decision taken in winter and a delivery schedule built for summer are two different commercial conversations.

From a foreign supplier's perspective the players that matter fall into a few groups: cash & carry chains led by METRO, delivered foodservice distributors, and specialist importers organised by product category. Which of them fits depends on product type, shelf life and the volume a supplier can commit to. This study sets out the size and structure of the market, profiles those groups, explains the market-access requirements for suppliers from the EU, from non-EU Europe and from outside Europe, identifies the product groups with the strongest prospects, and provides a directory of Greek importers and foodservice distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-hungary:
Hungarian out-of-home expenditure has been rising steadily and is projected to reach around €7.2 billion by 2028, up from about €6.2 billion in 2023, while total food-services revenue is expected to approach €8.2 billion — growing faster than expenditure itself. Persistent cost pressure at operator level makes private label and unbranded value products unusually relevant here, and pricing has to work after 27% VAT and any Public Health Product Tax before a listing becomes realistic.

Professional distribution is concentrated around a small number of players. METRO is the single most important, combining 13 self-service stores with national delivered foodservice, and its tiered own-brand programme is an explicit route in for a supplier without brand recognition in Hungary. Bidfood Hungary, established in 2021 as part of the global Bidcorp group, is scaling rapidly across HoReCa and catering. Below these sits a wide layer of category specialists. This study covers market size and structure, the three supply tiers that matter to a new entrant, the access requirements by supplier origin, and a directory of Hungarian importers and foodservice distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-india:
India's foodservice and restaurant market is broadly estimated at roughly USD 85 billion for 2025, with published estimates ranging from about USD 56 billion to USD 115 billion depending on how the informal sector is treated, and is projected toward roughly USD 140 billion by 2030 at about 10% compound annual growth. The drivers are structural rather than cyclical: urbanisation, rising disposable incomes and a young population that eats out more often than the generation before it.

What matters commercially for an exporter is that Indian demand has moved beyond basic commodities — consumer-oriented food imports reached roughly USD 8.4 billion in 2024 and have continued to grow — which is the segment where a branded or specialty foreign supplier can actually compete. This study sets out market size and structure under the competing definitions, profiles the importers, distributors and cash & carry operators that serve professional kitchens, explains the access requirements and documentation for foreign suppliers, identifies the product groups with the strongest prospects, and provides a directory of Indian importers and foodservice distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-indonesia:
Indonesia is the largest foodservice market in ASEAN. The USDA values the Hotel-Restaurant-Institutional sector at USD 29 billion for 2024, spread across some 231,500 outlets and now above pre-pandemic levels; broader models that include the informal segment reach far higher — USD 50.3 billion for 2025 with a forecast of USD 129.5 billion by 2034 (IMARC), or USD 62.4 billion for 2025 (Mordor Intelligence). For planning purposes the USDA figure is the most conservative and the most relevant, because it counts the outlets a foreign supplier can actually sell into.

The fundamentals behind that market are 282 million inhabitants, a young and urbanising population, and 13.9 million international visitors in 2024, including 2.4 million from Europe and 2.0 million from Oceania. Consumer-oriented food imports reached USD 8.6 billion in 2024, up from USD 8.3 billion. Digital ordering is not a side channel here: online food and beverage spending reached USD 12.9 billion in 2024, the largest e-commerce category in the country, with delivery alone accounting for USD 5.4 billion. This study includes a directory of Indonesian importers and foodservice distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-italy:
Italian foodservice is worth about €84 billion in 2025 and is the sixth-largest market in the world; counting the entire out-of-home chain across all channels, the estimate rises to about €101 billion. The growth recorded has been almost entirely price-driven rather than volume-driven. The operator landscape remains highly fragmented: 67% of companies have turnover below €2.5 million, and several hundred have left the market in recent years.

For a foreign supplier, the entry point is not the kitchen but the distributor. MARR, Gruppo DAC, Cateringross, METRO and Altasfera lead foodservice distribution and are all actively expanding their ranges, including private-label lines — often the fastest route for a new supplier. This study reconstructs the market's size and structure, the main players, the access requirements for EU, non-EU European and non-European suppliers, and the categories with the best prospects, and includes a directory of Italian HoReCa importers and distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-japan:
Japan's total food market was valued at roughly USD 421 billion in 2024, and foodservice is the larger half of it: about USD 228 billion, or 54%, against USD 193 billion in retail (USDA FAS). Hotel, restaurant and institutional foodservice sales reached about USD 226 billion in 2023, up roughly 16% year on year as dining out and inbound tourism recovered; independent market trackers place the foodservice market at approximately USD 256–289 billion for 2024–25, the spread reflecting different channel definitions rather than disagreement about direction.

For a foreign supplier, Japan rewards precision over volume: specification, consistency and documentation carry more weight in a listing decision than price alone. Cash & carry operators such as Gyomu Super (Kobe Bussan), A-Price and Hanamasa, along with the Costco club channel, serve independent operators, while delivered wholesalers and specialist importers cover the rest. This study sets out market size and structure, profiles the players that matter, explains the access requirements for suppliers from the EU, from non-EU Europe and from outside Europe, identifies the categories with the strongest prospects, and provides a directory of Japanese importers and foodservice distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-kingdom-of-bah:
The Kingdom of Bahrain is a compact but affluent Gulf market that imports the overwhelming majority of the food it consumes. For an export-oriented supplier of branded or private-label products, this import dependency is the central opportunity: almost everything on a hotel buffet, a restaurant menu or a café counter has reached the island through a local importer or distributor. Reaching Bahraini foodservice buyers therefore means, in practice, reaching the right importer or foodservice distributor.

Bahrain's foodservice (HoReCa) market is estimated at roughly USD 1.05 billion in 2025 and is widely forecast to grow at a double-digit compound annual rate through the end of the decade, driven by tourism, a young and growing expatriate population, rising eating-out habits and rapid expansion of quick-service and delivery formats. Quick-service restaurants dominate by value, while cloud kitchens and delivery are the fastest-growing segments.

The distribution landscape is led by a handful of long-established, full-range groups — Trafco, BMMI, Jawad Business Group, Ashraf's, Nass Foods and others — complemented by a dedicated broadline foodservice distributor (Bidfood Bahrain) and a set of category specialists in dry goods, dairy, frozen/chilled and meat. Cash-and-carry-style reach for smaller operators is provided mainly through hypermarket and supermarket groups such as LuLu and Al Jazira.

Market access is governed by the GCC-wide standards framework (GSO), mandatory halal certification for meat and animal-derived products, bilingual Arabic/English labelling, and health/food-safety documentation (ISO 22000 / HACCP being strongly preferred by serious buyers). EU suppliers and other non-GCC suppliers face broadly the same product and labelling requirements; the principal differences lie in tariff treatment, logistics and halal-body recognition, which are discussed in Section 6.

This study sets out the market size and structure, the leading players, the concrete opportunities for new foreign suppliers, and the access requirements — differentiated for EU, other non-EU and overseas suppliers — and closes with a working directory of the relevant HoReCa/foodservice importers, each with website and, where available, a general e-mail address and a central telephone number for first contact.
horeca-foodservice-market-latvia:
The Latvian food and beverage service industry recorded a production value of approximately EUR 995 million in 2023 according to Eurostat, up from around EUR 573 million in 2021 — a rise of more than EUR 420 million in two years. Few European markets of comparable size have moved that fast, and the growth has pulled in imported supply rather than displacing it, because domestic production cannot cover the range that operators now expect.

On the supply side, Bidfood Latvia is the leading dedicated HoReCa foodservice distributor, part of the international Bidcorp group and serving well over a thousand outlets, alongside operators such as Sanitex and PROMO Food Service that supply catering and institutional kitchens. For a foreign supplier the decision is which of these routes matches the product and the volume it can sustain. This study sets out market size and structure, profiles the distributors and cash & carry operators, explains the access requirements for suppliers from the EU, from non-EU Europe and from outside Europe, and provides a directory of Latvian importers and foodservice distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-lithuania:
Lithuania is a compact but steadily growing market of roughly 2.9 million inhabitants. On the narrower definition, the turnover of Lithuanian restaurants, cafés and catering reached about €1.67 billion in 2024, having grown by more than €0.7 billion since 2021. On the broader "food and drink service activities" definition the sector is estimated at roughly €3.2 billion for 2025–2026, spread across some 8,300 businesses — a reminder that published figures for this market differ mainly because of where the boundary is drawn.

For a foreign supplier the practical route runs through delivered foodservice distributors and cash & carry operators rather than through direct sales to kitchens, and the Baltic states are frequently served on an integrated basis, so a partner chosen in Lithuania may also carry a product into Latvia and Estonia. This study covers market size and structure, the leading players, the access requirements for suppliers from the EU, from non-EU Europe and from outside Europe, the product groups with the strongest prospects, and a directory of Lithuanian importers and foodservice distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-luxembourg:
Luxembourg is a small but exceptionally prosperous and international market. The Horesca federation represents around 2,900 establishments — from the smallest café to the largest hotel — employing more than 18,000 people; broader sector counts reach some 3,000 establishments and more than 20,000 employees. The country has more than 800 accommodation establishments and more than 15,000 hotel rooms, concentrated in and around Luxembourg City.

Within the Benelux out-of-home foodservice market, Luxembourg accounts for the smallest national share but the most dynamic one: growth is forecast at around 6% a year to 2031, faster than in Belgium or the Netherlands, driven by high disposable income, a compact urban geography that favours efficient delivery and a steady stream of tourists, business travellers and cross-border commuters. Cost pressure is real: automatic wage indexation regularly raises the cost of labour, compresses operators' margins and sharpens demand for products that save time in the kitchen or differentiate themselves clearly. This study includes a directory of Luxembourg importers and distributors in the sector.
horeca-foodservice-market-mauritius:
Mauritius has a resident population of about 1.26 million and a diversified economy spanning tourism, financial services, manufacturing and agriculture. Foodservice demand is anchored by tourism: roughly 1.44 million tourist arrivals in 2025, up 3.9% on the 1.38 million of 2024, with tourism receipts expected to exceed MUR 100 billion, about US$2.15 billion. Visitors outnumber residents, which is the single most important fact about this market.

That visitor base is served by a mature hotel and restaurant sector operating to international standards, which expects imported range as a matter of course since the island produces very little of what those kitchens use. For a foreign supplier the market is small in absolute volume but unusually accessible in specification terms, and the decision concentrates on a limited number of importers. This study covers market size and structure, profiles those importers and distributors, explains the access requirements and documentation for foreign suppliers, identifies the categories with the strongest prospects, and provides a directory of Mauritian importers and foodservice distribution partners.
horeca-foodservice-market-morocco:
Morocco is a mid-sized, developing and notably price-sensitive market: a population of approximately 37 million and GDP in the region of USD 140 billion, giving a modest but rising GDP per capita of about USD 3,400–3,900. The foodservice market is valued at approximately USD 3.4–3.5 billion across roughly 1,400–1,500 tracked businesses and is recovering toward its pre-pandemic level of around USD 5 billion.

Tourism is the engine and it is breaking records: after recovering from the pandemic, Morocco registered 17.4 million arrivals in 2024 and 19.8 million in 2025, overtaking Egypt as North Africa's leading destination, with a government target of 26 million visitors by 2030; tourism receipts reached about MAD 124 billion in 2025, roughly USD 13 billion, or some 7% of GDP. Consumer-oriented food imports run at roughly USD 2.7 billion a year, of which the European Union supplies about 53%, China 11%, the United States 6% and Switzerland 4% — a distribution that tells a European supplier its origin is already accepted here. This study includes a directory of Moroccan importers and foodservice distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-netherlands:
Dutch consumers spent around EUR 23 billion on eating and drinking out in 2025, 3.9% more than the previous year, with a forecast of roughly EUR 23.7 billion for 2026 (FSIN). Growth in recent years came mainly from price increases rather than from more visits. Koninklijke Horeca Nederland reported a hospitality turnover of EUR 33.9 billion for 2025 across some 43,600 establishments; the classic hospitality segment — restaurants, cafés, bars and hotels — accounts for about EUR 12.5 billion of that.

The wholesale layer is concentrated at the top and fragmented below. Sligro Food Group is the clear market leader with about a quarter of the foodservice market, distantly followed by HANOS, Bidfood and cash-and-carry operator Makro; the Foodservice Alliance estimates the foodservice wholesale market at around EUR 10.9 billion. For a foreign supplier, market access is therefore decided at the wholesaler or importer, not in the kitchen. This study covers market size and channel structure, the access requirements for suppliers from the EU and from outside it and the product groups with the best prospects, and includes a directory of Dutch importers and foodservice wholesalers.
horeca-foodservice-market-nigeria:
Nigeria is the largest consumer market in Africa, with a population well over 230 million and a young median age. Its foodservice market is valued at roughly USD 11.1 billion in 2025 and around USD 12.4 billion in 2026, with growth projected at a double-digit compound annual rate towards a market of over USD 21 billion by 2031. Few markets in the world combine that scale with that growth rate.

The practical questions for a foreign supplier are about mechanics rather than about demand: which importers hold the necessary registrations, how foreign-exchange availability and payment terms are handled, and which product formats and price points survive the local cold chain and the purchasing power of the target segment. This study sets out the size and structure of the market, profiles the importers, distributors and modern retail groups that serve hotels, restaurants and institutional kitchens, explains the access requirements, documentation and import formalities that apply to foreign suppliers, identifies the product groups with the strongest prospects, and provides a directory of Nigerian importers and distribution partners.
horeca-foodservice-market-norway:
Norway has a population of roughly 5.5 million, but per-capita food and out-of-home spending is high. The professional foodservice market — restaurants, hotels and institutional kitchens — is estimated to be worth in the order of NOK 90–110 billion, roughly EUR 7.5–9 billion. It is a small market by headcount and a substantial one by value, which changes what a foreign supplier should optimise for: margin and product fit rather than raw volume.

Norwegian grocery and foodservice supply is unusually concentrated in three vertically integrated groups — NorgesGruppen with its wholesale arm ASKO, Coop Norge and Reitan/REMA 1000 — which buy for both retail and the professional channel. Alongside them sits a layer of independent regional wholesalers organised in buying groups, one of which brings together around 13 to 14 regional members with a combined turnover of approximately EUR 400 million and is often the more realistic first door for a newcomer. This study covers market size and structure, the leading players, the access requirements for suppliers from the EU, from non-EU Europe and from outside Europe, and a directory of Norwegian importers and foodservice distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-oman:
Oman's national foodservice market is estimated at approximately USD 1.6–1.9 billion in 2025–2026 and is projected to reach roughly USD 2.4–3.0 billion by 2031, a compound annual growth rate in the region of 7.0 to 7.7%. It is the smallest of the Gulf markets covered in this series, and for that reason often the least contested by foreign suppliers.

The structural fact that matters is import dependence: Oman produces only a limited share of the processed food its kitchens use, so a foreign supplier is not displacing domestic production but competing with other importers on specification, price and reliability of supply. The route runs through importer-distributors that handle registration, customs and cold chain. This study sets out market size and structure, profiles those distributors, explains the access requirements and documentation for foreign suppliers including halal certification, identifies the product groups with the strongest prospects, and provides a directory of Omani importers and foodservice distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-peru:
Restaurant-channel sales in Peru are estimated at between USD 8,000 and 10,000 million, growing at an annual rate in the order of 7% to 10%, on a food retail market of approximately USD 23,000 million. Consumer-oriented food imports amount to around USD 1,900 million a year, a figure that shows how open the market is to foreign product.

Access runs through two main routes: cash & carry operators — Makro, Mayorsa and Corporación Vega — and the private-label programmes of the retail groups, which usually require less marketing investment than a brand launch and are decided on specification, price and audit. This study covers the volume and structure of the market, the main operators, the access requirements by supplier origin and the categories with the best prospects, and includes a directory of Peruvian importers and distributors in the HORECA channel.
horeca-foodservice-market-philippines:
Consumer foodservice sales in the Philippines are estimated at about US$14 billion on a 2024–2025 basis; broader definitions put the sector at roughly US$18–24 billion, but the narrower consumer-foodservice basis is the more useful one for a supplier deciding where to sell. The drivers are demographic and durable: a population of about 121 million growing at roughly 1.5% a year, rising household incomes, strong overseas-remittance inflows and a recovering tourism sector.

The number that matters most to an exporter is a different one: consumer-oriented agricultural imports into the Philippines totalled roughly US$9.8 billion in 2024. This is a market that already buys imported food at scale, so the competition is between origins and importers rather than against domestic supply. This study sets out market size and structure under both definitions, profiles the importers, distributors and cash & carry operators serving professional kitchens, explains the access requirements and documentation for foreign suppliers, identifies the categories with the strongest prospects, and provides a directory of Philippine importers and foodservice distribution partners.
horeca-foodservice-market-poland:
Published estimates of the Polish HoReCa market vary with definition and sit on the order of EUR 10–17 billion, growing at a mid-to-high single-digit rate. One commonly cited sizing puts the total at about USD 10.0 billion for 2024 with a compound annual growth rate near 6.55%, while restaurants and takeaways alone are projected at roughly EUR 17 billion across some 50,000 outlets by 2026. Tourism is one of the structural tailwinds: Poland recorded roughly 16.9 million foreign tourist arrivals in the most recent year measured.

Professional food distribution is controlled largely by delivered foodservice distributors — led by Bidfood Farutex, Chefs Culinar and Transgourmet Foodservice — together with the cash & carry operators Makro, Selgros and Eurocash. A useful feature for a foreign supplier is that several of the leading players are subsidiaries of large European groups (Bidcorp, Metro, Transgourmet/Coop, Chefs Culinar), so European supplier standards and documentation are already familiar on the buying side. This study covers market size and structure, the leading players, access requirements differentiated by supplier origin, and a directory of Polish importers and foodservice distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-portugal:
Portuguese commercial restaurants generated around EUR 14.5 billion in 2024, with average growth of approximately 2.9% a year between 2019 and 2024 and a projection of about EUR 17.1 billion by 2029. Restaurants and takeaway alone account for between EUR 11 and 12 billion, spread across more than 35,000 establishments — a high density and a highly fragmented business fabric.

For a foreign supplier, access is through the wholesaler. Makro, part of the METRO group, operates in cash & carry and develops private labels such as MasterChef, Gourmês and Amanhecer; Bidfood Portugal, part of the Bidcorp group and formerly Frustock, is the specialised distributor with the largest presence in the delivery channel. Being listed with one of these operators is the step that decides entry, not direct selling to the restaurant. This study presents the size and structure of the market, the main operators, the access requirements depending on the supplier's origin and the categories with the best prospects, and includes a directory of Portuguese importers and distributors in the HoReCa channel.
horeca-foodservice-market-qatar:
Independent market estimates converge on a Qatari foodservice market of about USD 2.0 billion in 2025, expanding at roughly 9% a year to approximately USD 3.1–3.35 billion by 2030–31. The broader food and beverage market, retail and foodservice combined, was worth on the order of USD 15 billion in 2024. Delivery is a substantial channel in its own right: consumers spent an estimated QAR 5.2 billion through delivery apps in 2024.

Qatar is a small market by population but a demanding one by specification, with a hotel and restaurant base built around international standards and a supply chain that depends on imports for most of what it serves. For a foreign supplier the practical route runs through importer-distributors that hold the necessary registrations and handle customs and cold chain. This study sets out market size and structure, profiles the distributors and specialist importers that serve professional kitchens, explains the access requirements and documentation for foreign suppliers including halal certification, identifies the product groups with the strongest prospects, and provides a directory of Qatari importers and foodservice distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-romania:
Romania's commercial foodservice sector was estimated at approximately RON 38 billion in 2023 — roughly USD 8.4 billion, or about EUR 7.5 billion in comparable food-services revenue terms — and is forecast to keep growing. The structural point for an exporter is the country's import dependence: agricultural and food imports reached around USD 15 billion in 2024, up roughly 4 to 5% year on year, with about 80% sourced from other EU member states, and the agri-food trade deficit widened to about EUR 4.8 billion. Local production cannot bridge seasonal gaps, so imported supply is not a marginal category here.

Two channels dominate professional supply. Cash-and-carry is led by Metro and Selgros, and above it sits a tier of large full-range importer-distributors — Interbrands Orbico, Macromex and Transilvania General Import among them — that handle importation, customs and national distribution on behalf of foreign brands. For a new supplier the practical question is which of the two routes fits the product and the volume ambition. This study covers market size and structure, the leading players, access requirements differentiated by supplier origin, the product groups with the strongest prospects, and a directory of Romanian importers and foodservice distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-slovakia:
Slovakia is a compact market of roughly 5.4 million people that functions, in practice, as part of an integrated Czech–Slovak market — which matters commercially, because several distributors buy and operate across both countries. Consumer foodservice generated on the order of €2.8 billion in revenue in 2023 and is forecast to grow towards roughly €3.5 billion by 2028, an annual rate of about 3 to 3.5%. Restaurants and takeaways alone account for around €1.6 billion across close to 11,800 businesses, with demand concentrated in Bratislava and Košice and a tourism component in the High Tatras.

The clear market leader in delivered foodservice is Bidfood Slovakia, part of the international Bidcorp group, which operates on an integrated Czech–Slovak basis and supplies well over 10,000 gastronomy outlets. In cash-and-carry, METRO Cash & Carry SR runs six large wholesale centres and is the reference operator. For a foreign supplier the integration with Czechia cuts both ways: a single conversation can open two markets, and a rejection can close both. This study covers market size and structure, the leading players, access requirements by supplier origin, and a directory of Slovak importers and foodservice distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-slovenia:
Slovenia is a compact EU and eurozone market of roughly 2.1 million residents, but its foodservice sector punches well above that headcount. The restaurant and foodservice market was estimated at about USD 1.14 billion in 2024 and is projected to grow at roughly 5.2% a year to around USD 1.77 billion by 2033, driven by record tourism and rising out-of-home consumption.

Retail is highly concentrated — Mercator, SPAR, Tuš, Lidl, Hofer, Eurospin and E.Leclerc — and several of these groups also run wholesale and cash & carry arms, so the same buying organisation can decide both a retail and a foodservice listing. Cash & carry is served by Mercator C&C and, notably, by METRO delivering cross-border from Croatia, a structural feature worth understanding before choosing a partner. This study covers market size and structure, the distribution channels, access requirements by supplier origin, the categories with the strongest prospects, and a directory of Slovenian importers and foodservice distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-spain:
Spain's commercial foodservice sector turns over on the order of EUR 130 billion a year according to 2025 estimates, after a sharp recovery in recent years. It is one of the largest hospitality markets in Europe relative to its population, sustained by both domestic consumption and tourism, and with an establishment density far above the European average.

Distribution is led by a handful of national operators and is organised along two routes. On one side cash & carry — Makro, GM Cash and Gros Mercat — where the hospitality operator buys on a self-service basis; on the other, full-range delivered distributors such as Bidfood, Pro a Pro, DDI and Qualianza. For a foreign supplier, entry is decided by getting listed with one of them, not by direct selling to the restaurant. This study covers market volume and structure, the leading operators, access requirements by supplier origin and the categories with the best prospects, and includes a directory of Spanish importers and distributors in the HORECA channel.
horeca-foodservice-market-thailand:
Thailand is one of ASEAN's most attractive and accessible foodservice markets. The Hotel-Restaurant-Institutional sector is estimated at approximately USD 35 billion in 2025 and is widely forecast to reach USD 50–55 billion within five to six years, implying compound annual growth in the region of 7 to 8%.

Supply reaches professional kitchens through three routes, and choosing the right one is the entry decision. Cash-and-carry and self-collect wholesalers — Makro and Go Wholesale — straddle retail and HoReCa and are the workhorse supply source for independent operators and SMEs. Full-range consumer-goods distributors serve both modern-trade retail and foodservice. And large operator groups buy centrally, among them PTT with its café and forecourt foodservice including Café Amazon, alongside international franchisors. This study sets out market size and structure, profiles those channels, explains the access requirements and documentation for foreign suppliers, identifies the product groups with the strongest prospects, and provides a directory of Thai importers and foodservice distribution partners.
horeca-foodservice-market-turkey:
Türkiye combines a young population of roughly 85 million, rapid urbanisation and a large, recovering inbound-tourism sector. Published estimates of the foodservice market vary more than in most countries and it is worth knowing why before quoting a number: they range from roughly USD 14–15 billion on a profit-sector basis (Mordor Intelligence) to about USD 23 billion (MarketLine, 2024) and up to some USD 44 billion on the widest definitions. The differences are about scope — which channels and which parts of the institutional sector are counted — rather than about disagreement on the market's direction.

For a foreign supplier the route runs through importer-distributors that handle customs, certification and national distribution; Bidfood Türkiye and g2m are leading examples of the professional foodservice tier. This study sets out market size and structure under each definition, profiles the players, explains the access requirements for suppliers from the EU, from non-EU Europe and from outside Europe — Türkiye's customs union with the EU matters here and is treated explicitly — identifies the categories with the strongest prospects, and provides a directory of Turkish importers and foodservice distributors.
horeca-foodservice-market-uruguay:
Uruguay is a compact, high-income economy with about 3.4 million residents. Its distinguishing feature for a supplier lies in tourism: the country received around 3.6 million visitors — more than its own resident population — with revenue close to USD 2,040 million. The supermarket sector turns over on the order of USD 2,500 million a year, a useful reference for sizing demand for packaged food.

Final consumer spending on restaurants is estimated on the order of USD 1,500 to 2,500 million a year. The range is deliberately wide: for a market of this size the available sources offer orders of magnitude rather than precise figures, and this study flags that wherever it occurs. The document covers the structure of the market and its channels, access requirements by supplier origin and the categories with the best prospects, and includes a directory of Uruguayan importers and distributors in the HORECA channel.
horeca-foodservice-market-vietnam:
Vietnam's foodservice market is estimated at roughly USD 24–25 billion in 2025 and is widely forecast to grow at a compound annual rate of about 9 to 11%, putting it on a path toward USD 41–54 billion within the next five to nine years. Growth is powered by a young and urbanising population, more than 18 million international arrivals, and the accelerating digitalisation of ordering and payment.

For a foreign supplier, Vietnam is at the stage where imported specialty and branded products are moving from the top-end hotel segment into the wider commercial restaurant base — which is the window in which an entrant can establish a position before the category is crowded. The route runs through licensed importers and distributors that handle registration, customs and cold chain. This study sets out market size and structure, profiles those partners, explains the access requirements and documentation for foreign suppliers, identifies the categories with the strongest prospects, and provides a directory of Vietnamese importers and foodservice distribution partners.
mercado-de-frutas-exoticas-alemania:
Alemania es uno de los mercados de fruta fresca más grandes y con mayor poder adquisitivo de Europa y, al carecer de producción tropical propia, depende casi por completo de la importación. Para los productores de África, Centroamérica y Sudamérica esto convierte al mercado en estructuralmente atractivo y, a la vez, muy competido y exigente. Las oportunidades no están en el negocio masivo de banano y piña, de margen bajo, sino en el segmento premium y de especialidades —sobre todo aguacate, frutos rojos, mango y maracuyá— y en los nichos ecológico y de comercio justo.

La certificación es en la práctica el billete de entrada: en lo legal, el certificado fitosanitario y el cumplimiento de los límites máximos de residuos; en lo comercial, GLOBALG.A.P. y GRASP y, sobre ellos, ecológico y/o Fairtrade o Rainforest Alliance. Para quien empieza, el camino pasa casi siempre por un importador establecido: suministrar directamente a las centrales de compra del comercio alemán —EDEKA Fruchtkontor, REWE Eurogroup— solo resulta realista con volumen, certificación completa y trayectoria demostrable. El factor decisivo es elegir importadores que realmente incorporen nuevos productores, y el listado de contactos de este estudio está filtrado y valorado con ese criterio.
plant-based-alternatives-germany:
Germany is Europe's largest market for plant-based alternatives and one of the most mature worldwide: meat, dairy and cheese alternatives have long since arrived on the mainstream shelf, the share of own-label products is rising and price pressure is increasing, while growth shifts from the niche into broad retail and foodservice. For a foreign manufacturer, what counts is therefore less the innovation lead than the ability to meet listing, logistics and labelling requirements in German retail.

This study sets out the market volume and channel structure for plant-based alternatives, names the leading retail and foodservice players, describes the access requirements and labelling rules for suppliers from the EU and from third countries, and includes a directory of German importers and distributors.
toy-market-france:
The French toy and games market reached around EUR 4.7 billion in 2025, up 7.1% in value and 7% in volume according to Circana — the strongest annual growth recorded in France since 2000, ahead of the United Kingdom (+6.1%) and Germany (+3.2%). A commercially important fact: this growth did not come from prices. The average price remained stable, at around EUR 18 over the year and EUR 21 during the Christmas period. Volumes, therefore, are what grew.

The momentum is concentrated in a few categories: strategic collectible cards (around +78%, led by Pokémon), construction (+32 to +35%, driven by LEGO), audio story players (+63%), card games (+16%) and traditional plush (+11%). Collecting, across categories, grew by around 45% and now accounts for nearly 13% of market value, while licences weigh around 30%. Distribution remains concentrated without being closed, with the toy specialist accounting for 37 to 44% of sales. This study is aimed at manufacturers and brand owners established outside France and includes a directory of French toy importers and distributors.
toy-market-italy:
The Italian market for traditional toys, excluding video games, is worth in the order of EUR 1.8–2.5 billion at retail depending on the measurement scope, while the video games market alone exceeds EUR 2 billion. Broadening the view to total spending on children and Gen Z — including clothing, publishing and licensed products — the estimated value exceeds EUR 7 billion.

Distribution does not run only through specialist shops. Large-scale retail chains — Esselunga, Coop, Conad, Selex — and non-food discounters absorb significant seasonal volumes and buy a great deal under private label, which opens a concrete door to a foreign supplier still without brand awareness in Italy. This study is aimed at manufacturers and brand owners based outside Italy, covers market size, channel structure and the technical and regulatory requirements for placing toys on the Italian market, and includes a list of importers, distributors and retailers that import on their own account.
toy-market-netherlands:
The Netherlands has around 18 million inhabitants with high household purchasing power, virtually full internet penetration and compact geography — a combination that makes nationwide distribution through a single partner realistic. The market for toys and games was valued at around USD 1.5 billion in 2025, equivalent to roughly EUR 1.4 billion, with expected growth to some USD 2.7 billion by the mid-2030s — annual growth of about 6 to 7%.

Within that market, the board games and puzzles segment is among the fastest growing, worth around USD 0.22 billion in 2025. For a foreign manufacturer or brand owner, the route to the shelf in the Netherlands almost always runs through an importer or distributor and not through the retailer itself. This study is written for suppliers of both branded products and private label, covers market size, channel structure and the legal and technical requirements for placing toys on the Dutch market, and includes an overview of Dutch importers, distributors and direct-importing retailers.
toy-market-portugal:
Portugal is one of the smallest toy markets in Western Europe, but stable. With a population of around 10.5 million, the toy and games market stands, at retail value, at around EUR 300 to 400 million a year. The range should be read as indicative: available sources measure on different bases — import value, retail value or a single subcategory — and published figures diverge considerably.

The supply structure depends heavily on imports, and Spain is by far the main supplier: around USD 141 million in dolls and toys, approximately 47% of the total imported. Marketplaces and online retailers, with Amazon.es serving the Portuguese market, are the fastest-growing channel. This study is aimed at manufacturers and brand owners based outside Portugal, discusses the size and structure of the market and the legal and technical requirements for placing toys on the Portuguese market, and includes a directory of importers, distributors and retailers that import on their own account.
toy-market-spain:
The Spanish market for traditional toys stands in a range of EUR 1,200 to 1,400 million in retail sales in recent years, and reaches EUR 1,500 million or more depending on the source and on whether video games and baby care items are included. Spain is Europe's fourth or fifth largest market by size, and published figures vary appreciably because each data provider measures on a different scope.

Distribution combines vertical toy chains with generalist large-format stores — Carrefour, Alcampo/Auchan — which buy relevant volumes of own brand and private label, a realistic entry route for a foreign manufacturer still without brand awareness in Spain. Between the product and the shelf there is almost always a Spanish importer or distributor, not the retailer directly. This study is aimed at manufacturers and brand owners established outside Spain, discusses the size and structure of the market and the legal and technical requirements for marketing toys, and includes a directory of importers, distributors and retailers that import on their own account.
toy-market-united-kingdom:
The United Kingdom is one of Europe's largest toy markets. The British Toy & Hobby Association and most of the trade value it at approximately £3.9 billion at retail; on Circana's European comparison the UK sits just over €5 billion, ahead of both France and Germany. Published figures differ widely because providers measure on different bases — retail against trade value, and varying treatment of trading cards, video games and licensed non-toy merchandise — which is why this study names the source behind every figure it quotes.

Two structural features shape the opening for a newcomer. Adult buyers are now the single largest segment: toys bought by and for people aged 12 and over grew about 5% in the twelve months to June 2025 and are worth roughly £1.2 billion, some 31% of total toy spend, or about £1 in every £3, with 43% of adults aged 18 and over buying toys for themselves. Preschool remains the volume engine at roughly 17% of spend and 22% of units, at an average purchase price near £8.54. This study is written for manufacturers and brand owners based outside the UK, whether branded or private-label, and its core is a directory of UK importers, distributors and direct-importing retailers that separates dedicated toy specialists from general non-food importers carrying toys as one category among many.
